news.title: ‘Pro-Palestine protests reshaping US politics’
news.text:
NEW YORK: Mahmoud Khalil, who became the face of resistance to President Donald Trump’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian student activism, believes the movement has succeeded by shifting public perception and encouraging a generation of leaders ready to question views about Israel.

“The American public is finally changing, is finally looking at the Palestinian as an equal human,” the 31-year-old said in an interview one week before crucial midterm elections — and just as Israel held its own election.

Khalil rose to prominence when he helped lead demonstrations at New York’s Columbia University, the epicentre of protests against the war in Gaza that swept US campuses in 2024. At the height of Trump’s crackdown, immigration authorities responded by detaining Khalil — a permanent US resident born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria — for three months without criminal charge, making him miss the birth of his first child. But despite the personal toll — recounted in his memoir “No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention” — Khalil credited Palestinian advocacy with helping to transform public opinion in the United States, where polls show historic growth in support for Palestinians. “This gives me hope,” he said in his New York apartment.

“Also, we can see on the ground that we have more progressive candidates being elected into Congress and positions of power.” Khalil pointed to Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim running for US Senate in the key state of Michigan, as well as pro-Palestinian New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was elected last year.

Both men are also notably critics of Israel — a move away from the traditional defence of the US ally among both Republicans and Democrats.

‘Work not done yet’

Khalil said that Trump sought to “chill” free speech on Palestinian rig--hts with his arrest — which the president celebrated in a social me-d--ia post, saying it was the first of ma--ny to come. “The Trump administration tried to dehumanise me for my advocacy for Palestine, for my opp--o-sition to the genocide in Gaza,” he said.

“It was clear to me that this administration just wanted to make an example out of me, so people wouldn’t speak out for Palestine.” The Trump administration says it is fighting anti-Semitism and illegal immigration, using both arguments to justify everything from controversial detentions of activists to defunding elite universities where pro-Palestinian protests took place. Khalil said that strategy backfired.

“The fact that the president of the United States came after me, a random student, means that I was doing something right,” he added.

‘Such cruelty’

Khalil’s ordeal also exposed him to conditions in a Louisiana jail he likened to torture, describing constant fluorescent light, cold, and poor food. “I never imagined that such cruelty is happening on US soil,” Khalil said of the deportation drive led by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“I came to a country that supposedly champions liberty, justice, rule of law, only to be shocked when I entered these detention centers that all my rights were left outside,” he said. Khalil has been free for well over a year but the Trump administration is still pushing for his deportation even as he raises his son, now aged 18 months, in New York with his wife. It’s an emotional cost that is hard to bear.

Published in Dawn, October 29th, 2026

news.title: Now Corruption in Brazil Is a 'Conspiracy Theory'
news.text:
Runoffs in Brazil's presidential elections took place this past Sunday, Oct. 25, and the socialist candidate — Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ("Lula") — won after some procedural funny business. Among other things, Lula's campaign claimed that traffic congestion prevented some voters on city buses from getting to the polls before they closed at 5 PM. Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, who has also been Lula's private attorney and was appointed to the Supreme Court by Lula, unilaterally issued an order demanding that the polls be reopened for two hours — but only in pro-Lula districts. In parts of the country that favored Lula's opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, polls remained closed. Zanin's decision was also problematic because the country has an electoral court with exclusive jurisdiction over election procedures; Zanin does not sit on that court.

Lula ended up winning — a remarkable result, given that he had trailed Bolsonaro by 2 million votes in the first election round a few weeks prior. Never in modern Brazilian history has a presidential candidate who came in second in the first round of voting won in the runoff.

But that's not the worst part. Bolsonaro objected to the results and declared his intention to have the election investigated, whereupon Senhor Presidente Lula called for Bolsonaro's arrest and demanded that he surrender his passport.

How very democratic. This is the way a politician behaves when he is confident about his victory, right? He immediately orders the arrest of his opponent?

Bolsonaro knew what was coming; his father was arrested by Lula and is currently serving a 27-year sentence. He apparently reached out to his contacts in Argentina and here in the United States (Secretary of State Marco Rubio is said to have played a role in Bolsonaro's escape). According to Reuters, Bolsonaro, his wife, Fernanda, and their two daughters crossed (passports in hand) into the Misiones province in Argentina late on Tuesday, Oct. 27, and boarded a private jet that took them to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and then on to Miami, Florida. Although Argentinian President Javier Milei has not released an official statement, Bolsonaro publicly thanked both President Donald Trump and Milei upon his arrival in Florida. The Bolsonaros will be given visas to stay in the United States.

Trump weighed in on the matter, saying, "It looked like another rigged election, frankly. I didn't take sides, but it was a terrible look for the world. Elections have to be indisputable, and it looked really bad to me."

Right on cue, here came America's left-leaning legacy media. An NBC News post on X Tuesday read, "Although Brazil's presidential election took place more than 4,000 miles away, the baseless conspiracy theory that it was stolen raced through the American right-wing media."

We'll let the investigative process (such as it is) play out in Brazil. But allow me to remind you of just a few of the events our media have told us were "baseless conspiracy theories" in recent years:

That COVID-19 was accidentally released from a lab at the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China.That "gain-of-function" virus research was being conducted in China and funded by the United States government.That mRNA shots didn't prevent contraction or transmission of COVID-19.That those same shots had harmful — even deadly — side effects, like myocarditis and pericarditisThat the drug ivermectin helped treat COVID-19 and isn't just "horse paste."That social media companies like Facebook and Twitter (pre-Elon Musk's purchase of the platform) were censoring facts and keeping truthful information from the public at the request of the Obama and Biden administrations.That Hunter Biden's laptop was not "Russian disinformation" and did, in fact, contain images of him using drugs and with prostitutes — including some that looked underage — and emails showing that Hunter was selling access to his father, former President Joe Biden.That the Obama and Biden administrations were weaponizing law enforcement against Trump and violating his constitutional rights (as well as those of members of his campaign team and Cabinet) by fabricating allegations of collusion with Russia that they knew were false.That federal law enforcement under the Obama administration lied to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to illegally obtain surveillance warrants.That Hillary Clinton's campaign illegally paid for "opposition research" that was used to fabricate allegations against Trump that everyone knew were false.That there were election abnormalities in the 2020 election.That there were federal agents in the crowds at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

Shall I continue?

Most of the legacy media outlets in this country are less investigative journalism organizations than they are vehicles for largely left-wing propaganda. And you know what that means: "This is extremely dangerous to our democracy."

What's more shocking — but shouldn't be at this point, frankly — is how many on the left in this country are taking Lula's side. Our reliably ill-informed celebrities in Hollywood have appeared in videos supporting him, making "L's" with their thumb and forefinger. (In my lifetime, that symbol has had a different meaning, and one that seems remarkably appropriate for those making the gesture now.) Democrat politicians like Congressman Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) and outgoing Congressman Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.) have supported Lula for demanding Bolsonaro's passport and attempting to throw him in prison.

Why should I be surprised? This is the same party that attempted to frame Trump on false charges of "colluding" with Russia, engaged in illegal surveillance of his campaign, and cheered on a New York state judge who idiotically lowballed the value of Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort at $18 million to $27 million so he could find Trump guilty of fraud in borrowing against the property (and repaying the loan in full — with interest, no less). Mar-a-Lago is nearly 20 acres of unparalleled waterfront real estate in Palm Beach, Florida — an island where property runs $30 million to $44 million per acre. At a conservative estimate of $25 million per acre, Mar-a-Lago is worth $500 million.

Corruption in Brazil looks eerily similar to corruption in the United States, and its cheerleaders are on the same political side.

news.title: President Trump: Cheerleader-In-Chief
news.text:
In 2014, President Barack Obama, during the last midterm of his presidency, was 53 years old. He did seven rallies, four of which took place in October. In 2022, President Joe Biden, during his only midterm election, was 79 years old. He largely avoided traditional rallies. President Donald Trump, during the last midterm of his presidency, is 80 years old. So far in this month of October, he has held 23 rallies.

Biden was widely criticized for failing to do more campaigning. ABC News' Jonathan Karl asked Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-NY), then-chair of the House Democrats' campaign arm, why Biden was not hitting the campaign trail harder. Maloney replied, "I don't know what you're talking about."

Maloney described a Biden campaign stop in his district in Poughkeepsie, New York. Karl was unimpressed: "I recall in 2010 President Obama doing 16 rallies all across the country in the month of October alone."

As for President Obama, in October 2014, his approval rating was at 40%, according to an ABC/Washington Post poll, the lowest score in that poll since Obama entered office. Two weeks before the 2014 midterms, CNN wrote, "President Barack Obama says his feelings aren't hurt by Democrats who don't want to campaign side-by-side with him because those candidates are 'strong allies and supportive of me' when casting votes in Congress. ... Obama's remarks could harm endangered red-state Democrats and offer a boost to Republicans who need to capture six seats to gain control of the Senate for the president's final two years in office."

After the huge 2014 Democratic congressional losses, the liberal outlet Salon slammed Democrats for distancing themselves from Obama: "Nine times out of 10, if a Democrat runs a race in which she or he is constantly apologizing for being a Democrat, voters will simply opt to elect a Republican. Obama may be deeply unpopular in Kentucky, West Virginia and Alaska, but in a competition over who sticks it to the president more, guess which party will always come out on top."

This is exactly how Trump sees it.

He confidently tells voters, "Act like I'm on the ballot," something Democrats, given his poll numbers, are practically giddy to hear. But Trump vigorously defends his record on the economy, the Iran War, crime, the border and on deportations. He denounces the rise of socialism within the Democrat Party and Medicare for All, considered the signature policy issue for many congressional Democrats and Democrat candidates. Even the Washington Post editorial board calls it "taxes for all."

Trump noted that just days ago, despite the gloomy predictions by economic experts, the consumer confidence index increased in October, and the September index was revised upward. Inflation adjusted median household income in 2025 reached an all-time high. Poverty in 2025 stood at a record low. Despite the dreary headlines, consumers continue to spend. The national average price of a gallon of regular gas remains lower than its peak under Biden.

Market Watch recently wrote:

"The economy is poised to show a growth rate of 3% or more from July to September when the government next week reports gross domestic product for the third quarter. The U.S. might even be on track to post frothy annual growth of 2.5% in 2026. It wasn't supposed to happen.

"Many economists predicted growth would slow after the spring as spending from large tax refunds dried up and the U.S.-hosted World Cup ended. High oil prices, rising inflation, the lingering effect of tariffs and the ongoing conflict in Iran were expected to depress growth. Instead, consumer spending picked up and businesses boosted investment."

Trump's approval rating is lower than that of Obama's 40 percent in October 2014, and lower than that of Biden's 40 percent in October 2022. The New York Times Presidential Approval Tracker places Trump's approval at 36 percent, a record low for his presidency. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll shows his approval rating at 32 percent, a 1-point improvement from the previous week's record low.

Yet, love him or hate him, Trump knows his best campaign surrogate cheerleader is Trump. His October schedule of rallies, meetings, policy briefings, media appearances and travel is absolutely exhausting.

No matter what happens on Nov. 3, even Trump's detractors should acknowledge this: The man stood by his record. He did not mail it in.

news.title: The Midterms Are Either the Most or Least Important Elections Ever
news.text:
I don’t know what’s going to happen in the midterms, and you don’t know what’s going to happen in the midterms, and the boosters and pundits certainly don’t know what’s going to happen in the midterms. But something is going to happen in the midterms. And what happens in the midterms will make them either the most important midterms in the history of ever, or the least important. It all depends. Which means you shouldn’t take a chance, and you should get out there and vote all red just in case.

There is a substantial chance that these will be the least important midterms ever. Now, I know we’re not supposed to say that. I know we’re supposed to treat everything as if it’s existential, and there’s certainly the potential for existentiality here. But if the Republicans keep both houses of Congress, it’s going to turn out not to be a very important midterm. And, if the Republicans lose the House, particularly by a small margin – this seems to be the historically likely outcome – then it also won’t be that important in retrospect.

What do I mean? I mean, having Hakeem Jeffries wrangling the herd of cats that is a Democrat majority in the House of Representatives is a fate I wouldn’t wish upon anybody except a Democrat, which is convenient. The fact is, if they take the House, what are they going to do? On the legislative side, Donald Trump’s signature legislation has already gone through. President Trump passed the Big Beautiful Bill. We got the tax cuts, and we funded ICE for the foreseeable future. I guess they can pass a bunch of pinko-commie wishlist bills, like socialized medicine, defunding the police, and demanding that the United States withdraw from North America, but who cares? That kind of onanism won’t go anywhere in the Senate if we keep it. And I think we will probably keep it.

But even if we don’t keep it, President Trump will still have his veto. Look for the veto to become a leftist bugaboo like the Electoral College, the Supreme Court, and heterosexuality. They can pass all the neo-Marxist bills they want, which Trump will veto. And they’ll stand there, looking stupid, a do-nothing Congress that is merely a spectator to the president’s pen-and-phone governance.

They’ll be stuck passing their pet bills merely to make a point, but the message they send may not play well outside of coastal California, Manhattan, and blue inner-city congressional districts. Much of the stuff they will pass is pure poison out in real America, but even the alleged moderates are going to have to get aboard because the Democrat majority’s margin is going to be so thin that it needs to be all hands on deck on the political Titanic. That means people who got elected pretending to be normal are going to have to vote for crazy things. Are they going to try to tell the mouth-breathing psychopath Democrat base that they couldn’t pass the DSA’s wishlist? Do you think that the DSA types are going to accept that President Trump will veto whatever they send him as a reason not to send him their kooky legislation? This election cycle, one of the things that has helped the Democrats is the fact that they haven’t actually done anything. Oh, they’ve said lots of stuff about transing kids, opening the borders, and so on, but once they get a majority, their own party is going to force them to take actual votes. All those people pulling the Spanberger Moderate Campaign Game™ are going to get stuck voting for this wacky nonsense. And next election cycle, their Republican opponents will use it as an electoral suppository.

This is not to say that losing won’t have negative consequences. It’s just that those consequences aren’t apocalyptic, at least not in the short term. And there’s lemonade to be made from lost election lemons. If the Republicans lose the House, Trump has something that he’s uniquely suited to using to his advantage — a nemesis he can play against.

Losing the Senate is a bigger deal because the Senate ratifies nominations. A Democrat Senate will refuse to allow Trump to hire subordinates as a way to refuse to allow Trump to govern. The Democrats are of the opinion that the American people had no right to elect Donald Trump, and that anything he does is illegitimate, and therefore they have no obligation to even consider his appointees. Their only purpose will be to destroy him and disenfranchise his voters. Don’t expect any nominee to be confirmed to any office, not one judge, ambassador, or secretary. And that would be a problem for the administration, though not insurmountable.

But it would also be a problem for the Democrats. The American people have limited patience for that kind of shenanigans. Remember, Donald Trump is going to be looking to 2028, not for himself but for his legacy. If he has one or two houses of Congress in opposition, he’s going to highlight their knee-jerk rejection of his most common-sense and popular proposals. And when the economy inevitably improves and the Iran War resolves, then things are going to start getting better. It’ll be the Democrats’ turn to demand that voters not believe their lying eyes. Remember 1982? Reagan got creamed in the midterms. But what happened in 1984? Two years later, the economy was cranking, and it was morning in America. Ronald Reagan won 49 states.

Moreover, in opposition, the congressional and Senate Republicans are going to look better and better. Their big problem this year is that when the Republicans had the majority in both houses, they did not do much after the first year. In opposition, at least they’ll have an excuse for not doing anything. Throwing the GOP into the trunk will, ironically, probably do them a world of good. In politics, absence makes the heart grow fonder, and no one excels like the Republicans in meeting the expectations of people who have low expectations.

But the Democrats will exploit any power they have. For example, there’s the threat of impeachment and investigations. Please bring on the impeachments. They just spent a whole cycle talking about how Trump is refusing to focus on affordability. Well, it doesn’t make a lot of sense to then spend the next two years focusing on the exercise in windmill jousting that is another impeachment — or impeachments. It’s all a show, and a stupid one. If we hold the Senate, the House will have its festival of judicial onanism and then walk over with the impeachment documents; John Thune — if he knows what’s good for him politically — will take them and throw them in the trash just like the Democrats did with the Mayorkas impeachment. And if the Democrats take the Senate, they can have their Senate trial, and they will still lose. Even the weakest Republican is going to look at what happened to Bill Cassidy after he supported impeachment and vote no.

Impeachment is a loser’s game. Ask the Republicans whether it’s a good plan to try to lose your way to victory.

There will be lots of investigations and lots of kangaroo committees trying to frame Trump and those who work for him for imaginary crimes. If the Democrats are smart, which is a big if — they are the Chauncey Gardiners of American politics — they will focus on a few select targets. But what do you think the chances are that they’re going to be disciplined and focused? And what do you think the chances are that Donald Trump’s DOJ is going to bring charges against someone who refuses to testify or respond to a Dem subpoena? The only thing these investigations are going to result in is adding names to Trump’s preemptive pardon list.

But here’s the real danger and the reason why this election could be hugely important. It sets up the map for the 2028 election. If they do well now, they’re in a better position to win in 2028. We know what the Democrats are going to do if they get a trifecta. They’re going to end the filibuster and attempt to change the government once and for all such that they can never lose power again. Now, that’s a fool’s errand, and it won’t work, but the danger is that in their attempts to crush democracy in favor of perpetual democratocracy, they will permanently damage the constitutional order of this country. There’s approximately a 0 percent chance that normal Americans will look at a Democrat administration backed up by a Democrat Congress that has packed the Supreme Court with ventriloquist dummies who tell them that they don’t have free speech, freedom of religion, or the right to keep and bear arms, and just sort of give in. You’re looking at chaos. If you want to preview the chaos, pre-order my new novel, American Warlord (it comes out on Tuesday, Election Day) to see how the worst-case scenario plays out.

So, the real importance of 2026 is how it affects 2028. This election will tee up that one. And if we end up in a hole that we can’t dig out of next cycle, then this will truly be the most important midterm election ever.

news.title: Bolsonaro’s self-declaration poses no threat to Lula’s presidency — Brazilian congressman
news.text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 29. /TASS/. The attempts by Flavio Bolsonaro, a Brazilian senator who has fled to the United States, to contest the result of Sunday’s election and declare himself "the elected president" do not pose a threat to the government of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a Brazilian lawmaker told TASS.

"He (Bolsonaro - TASS) will remain in isolation in the international arena because almost all countries have already congratulated Lula [da Silva] on winning the election, including our neighbors in Latin America," Francisco (Chico) de Alencar, a federal deputy of the republic’s National Congress, argued.

According to the legislator, Bolsonaro’s move will not find actual support globally. "Nor will [US President] Donald Trump help him either. I can say for sure that they (the United States - TASS) actually do not have a good opportunity for any interference in Brazil’s [affairs]," he emphasized.

Earlier, Flavio Bolsonaro fled to the United States where he declared himself "the elected president" in an open letter. Around an hour later, he changed his title to the South African republic’s "leader" and deleted his previous self-declaration.

Brazil held a presidential runoff on October 25. According to the final results released by the electoral commission, incumbent President Lula da Silva won the election with 51.79% of the vote, while Flavio Bolsonaro lost with 48.21%. The president-elect criticized his rival's departure as "shameful."
news.summary: According to the legislator, Flavio Bolsonaro’s move will not find actual support globally

news.title: US judge handling deposed Venezuelan president Maduro's case dies
news.text:
NEW YORK: Alvin Hellerstein, the US judge overseeing the case against deposed Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, has died aged 92, an official confirmed on Wednesday.

As one of the oldest US federal judges, questions had been raised about whether he was the right justice to preside over what could be a prolonged trial for Maduro on drug trafficking charges.

Hellerstein’s lengthy career included overseeing the civil cases arising from Al Qaeda’s Sept 11, 2001 terrorist attacks on New York and Washington, often rejecting deals he saw as unfair to complainants.

His death was confirmed by an official at the United States District Court, Southern District of New York, where he presided. Hellerstein also tangled with Donald Trump, rejecting a request by the US president to have his New York hush money case moved to federal court. Last year, he blocked the Trump administration from deporting alleged Venezuelan gang members without a court hearing.

In a noteworthy 2015 ruling, Hellerstein ordered the US government to release a trove of photos depicting abuse of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan. He also presided over a trial last year in which a jury found French banking giant BNP Paribas’s work in Sudan had helped prop up the regime of former ruler Omar al-Bashir, awarding $20.75 million in damages to three plaintiffs from Sudan.

Hellerstein handled the sprawling drug trafficking case linked to Maduro for over a decade, which has already seen the conviction of Venezuela’s former intelligence chief, Hugo Armando Carvajal.

Maduro was seized by US forces in January in a military raid on his compound in Venezuela. A graduate of Columbia University law school, Hellerstein served as a lawyer in the US Army from 1957 to 1960 before entering private practice.

He was nominated by then president Bill Clinton in 1998 to be a district court judge for the Southern District of New York.

news.title: Haley Stevens Backs Abdul El-Sayed Despite Fiancé's Rogers Endorsement
news.text: In a display of party unity in the fiercely contested battle for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, former Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens said she plans to vote for Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, despite losing to him in the primary and her fiancé's public back of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Appearing on CNN with Kaitlan Collins Wednesday night, Stevens was asked about her fiancé's decision to support Rogers, the former congressman and FBI agent who emerged as the Republican nominee. “Like a lot of households across America, we’re a household divided,” Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the August Democratic primary, said on CNN. "I still very much want our Democratic nominee, his name is Abdul, to win this race, there's so much on the line.” Stevens underscored her support for Democrats and El-Sayed, her former primary rival, as he faces Rogers in a race that could help determine control of the U.S. Senate. “I want our Democrats to win, I want to see Abdul do the right thing here," she said. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, described his decision to vote for Rogers over El-Sayed as “putting country before party.” Turkish, a civil rights attorney, told The Detroit News that he had witnessed “an escalation in [El-Sayed’s] rhetoric since the primary, and it makes folks unsafe.” He added, "Every time he talks about genocide (in Gaza), Jews get death threats." When asked about Turkish's decision to support Rogers out of concerns over Israel, El-Sayed said the election was about control of the Senate and checking President Donald Trump. “If folks see another issue that is more important to them and decide that their disagreement with me on that is bigger than their agreement with me on all these other things, that is their choice,” El-Sayed told reporters Wednesday night. Newsweek reached out to the Rogers campaign for comment late Wednesday night. U.S. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas campaigned alongside Rogers at a rally in Bad Axe, Michigan, on Wednesday, urging voters to support the Republican nominee while criticizing El-Sayed. “We cannot let Michigan fall to a communist with Muslim Brotherhood ties,” Cruz wrote on X. Cruz also reacted to The Detroit News report about Turkish’s endorsement of Rogers, sharing the article on X alongside an eyes emoji. Democrats Look to the General Election The Michigan Senate race is expected to be among the most closely watched contests of the 2026 midterm cycle. El-Sayed, a progressive who first gained statewide attention during his 2018 gubernatorial campaign, won the Democratic nomination after running on issues including healthcare, economic inequality and opposition to U.S. support for Israel's war in Gaza. Rogers entered the general election with strong support from national Republicans and has sought to frame himself as an experienced national-security voice capable of appealing to both conservatives and swing voters. For Democrats, Stevens' endorsement of El-Sayed may be less significant for the votes it delivers than for what it symbolizes: Primary losers are often pressured to help unite their party, particularly in battleground states such as Michigan. What Polls Show Polling averages show a close race between El-Sayed and Rogers. RealClearPolitics rates the Michigan U.S. Senate race as a toss-up, with its polling average showing El-Sayed leading Rogers by 2.8 percentage points, 48.8 percent to 46 percent, as of Tuesday. A CBS News/Mitchell poll conducted on October 26 and October 27 found El-Sayed ahead by 7 points, 51 percent to 44 percent, outside the poll's 3.9-point margin of error. A Detroit News/Glengariff poll conducted from October 19 to October 22 showed El-Sayed leading 51 percent to 45 percent, also outside the 4-point margin of error, while a Marist poll conducted from October 15 to October 18 found him ahead 50 percent to 48 percent, within the 4.3-point margin of error. More than 1.39 million Michigan voters had cast their ballots as of Tuesday, according to the Michigan secretary of state. news.summary: The former Democratic Senate candidate plans to support her former rival, saying, “We’re a household divided.”
news.author: Alex Backus,Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: Bloomberg, two trading firms agree to pay Trump’s Truth Social for faster access to president’s posts, sources say
news.text: NEW ​YORK Susquehanna and Jump Trading among customers of Truth API service, sources say Subscribers pay between $60,000 and $100,000 a month for the service Trump Media says there is ‘significant demand’ for the fast access to posts Critics see legal and ethical issues with pay-for-access Truth Social, the social media platform founded by President Donald Trump, has signed up news and data provider Bloomberg and two Wall Street firms for ‌faster access to the president’s posts, which it sells for up to $100,000 a month, according to people with direct knowledge ​of the matter. The firms are Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading, both high-frequency trading firms focused on algorithmic and automated strategies. The ⁠service gives subscribers a timing advantage to Trump’s posts on Truth Social, which has the potential to create swings in financial markets and to give Wall Street traders an edge not available to everyday investors. The companies’ purchase of the Truth API service hasn’t been previously reported. An API is a programming interface that is used as ‌a digital bridge that allows one system to connect to another. Trump Media and Technology Group announced its fastest-access product in July, and pitched it to trading firms and other financial institutions. The deals likely mark the first time a business tied to a ‌sitting president has sold access to their statements, which some critics have called unethical. While Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan ventures into untested legal territory, Intercept ‌Media ⁠and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump in August, seeking to block the White House from posting official government ⁠announcements exclusively on Truth Social while the paid feed exists. The suit, which is ongoing, alleges that erecting a financial barrier to government information is potentially unconstitutional and favors wealthy Wall Street firms. Bloomberg, Jump Trading and Susquehanna declined to comment. In a statement, Trump Media said: “Truth Social offers an industry-standard API product for which there is significant demand across industries. We take customer confidentiality seriously. ​This reporting is based on misleading information being peddled by anonymous ‌sources aimed at harming our company, customers and shareholders.” The president’s family trust owns 41% of Trump Media, and Trump is the trust’s sole beneficiary. Shares of the company have fallen more than 50% so far this year. The market value of Trump Media has been volatile since it went public; it closed at about $8 billion in its March 2024 debut, but is now worth about $1.8 billion. The company has lost about $1.76 billion ‌since 2024, including non-cash charges. Trump Media’s Securities and Exchange Commission filings listTrump, Jr., as the trustee of the family trust, with ​sole voting and investment power. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said neither Trump nor his family is directly involved in any portfolio investment decisions but did not address the allegations that the president was improperly using his office. Trump Jr. did not respond ⁠to a comment request. Questions about his role in the business were referred to the Trump Organization, which did not respond to requests for comment. MARKET-MOVING POSTS The service is designed to allow customers to read Trump’s posts more quickly than a human would by constantly checking the app. The timing advantage, described as ‌50 milliseconds by Trump Media officials, can matter to trading firms or financial news and data organizations because a US president’s posts can create swings in the value of assets. High-frequency Wall Street traders employ software that ingests news headlines, company announcements and government statements to search for market-moving information. The software can read, analyze and execute a trade in thousandths of a second. In one example of how Trump’s posts can move markets, oil futures sank after he announced on Truth Social a ceasefire in the Iran war in April. In August, Trump Media told investors it had “signed more than 10 customer agreements” which Reuters was unable to confirm. The company didn’t name the clients, but said they were primarily Wall Street trading firms that are paying between $60,000 and $100,000 a month. Reuters, ‌a financial-news competitor to Bloomberg, said in a statement: “We will assess the service, but have no current plans to subscribe.” Selling faster access to Trump’s posts has drawn criticism from Democrats ​and media entities. Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and California’s Adam Schiff said in July that they had asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the service violated securities laws. They described it as a “shocking abuse” of office ⁠by a president seeking personal gain, without providing further explanation. The SEC declined to comment. A TMTG spokesperson said, “Congressional Democrats continue to mischaracterize Truth API either out of ⁠ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.” In the lawsuit against Trump by Intercept Media and non-profit Freedom of the Press Foundation, the plaintiffs described the paid data service as “profoundly corrupt.” The suit also alleges the service ‌would violate the First Amendment rights of the public who don’t have equal access to the information and it would violate the Fifth Amendment by charging “unreasonable sums” for equal access to information guaranteed by law. The White House’s Ingle did not directly address the lawsuit or its allegations, saying, “President ​Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office.” Susquehanna and Jump Trading among customers of Truth API service, sources say Subscribers pay between $60,000 and $100,000 a month for the service Trump Media says there is ‘significant demand’ for the fast access to posts Critics see legal and ethical issues with pay-for-access
news.summary: The service gives subscribers a timing edge on Trump’s Truth Social posts, potentially moving markets and giving Wall Street traders an edge not available to everyday investors
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Are the midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
news.text:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 US election against Kamala Harris, he pulled together a coalition of voters that don't have much history voting Republican.

Working class and lower income voters helped deliver him key swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while Hispanic voters helped turn the sun belt states of Arizona and Nevada red.

Research from Pew found that Trump voters were markedly more racially and ethnically diverse in 2024 (20 per cent non-white) than they were in 2020 (14 per cent) and 2016 (10 per cent).

Virtually all demographic groups swung to Trump in 2024, but a New York Times analysis concluded the biggest shifts were among young Black and Hispanic voters.

At the time of that election, strategists wondered if Trump had catalysed a political realignment in the country that would continue to work in Republicans' favour.

But converting irregular voters into reliable members of the Republican base is not easy.

Two years on, as the cost of living bites, they don't appear to have stuck around, and the Hispanic voters that swung behind Trump have either swung right back to the Democrats, or are choosing to sit this election out.

The Republican Party appears almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives in next week's midterm elections. Democrats also lead in polls in more than enough Senate races to be able to take control of that chamber as well (although many of those leads are within the margin of error).

Among the list of prizes that Democrats are hoping to pick up next week, the state of Texas glistens seductively.

Democrats haven't won a senate seat in the state since 1988, but this year, their candidate James Talarico is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in polling.

Republicans appear to be vulnerable in deep red states, and in recent weeks Trump has held rallies on Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and Alabama. That is not the strategy of a party that's feeling confident.

Donald Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but at rallies he has repeatedly asked voters to "pretend" he is.

"They say that Trump does great when he's on the ballot, but when he's not on the ballot … his people don't come and they don't vote for senators, congressmen," he said at a rally in South Carolina in August.

Part of the Trump campaign's strategy in 2024 was to increase turnout rates among people who would usually stay home. Among the group of people who voted in that election but not in 2020, Pew estimated Trump had a 12 percentage point lead over Harris.

High turnout helped him two years ago. This year, it may be part of his undoing.

Trump wants voters to be thinking about him when they consider voting, because last time that drove lots of people to the polls.

The trouble is that, in 2026, the president is very unpopular.

Nobody's ever seen a president so disliked

American politicians are, as a general rule, held in much lower regard now than they used to be. But amidst an unpopular bunch, Donald Trump is reaching new depths.

YouGov and the Economist have been regularly tracking views on US presidents by asking voters whether they approve or disapprove of the job the leader is doing.

In his first term, Trump was into net negative territory effectively from the moment he took office. President Biden was in the negatives within seven months.

But in his second term, Trump has plummeted. A week out from polling day, the Economist recorded a net approval rating of -27, with 34 per cent of voters approving of the job he's doing and 61 per cent disapproving.

That is a lower net approval rating than any other president has recorded just before their midterm elections since World War II.

Given the president's party nearly always goes backwards in the House of Representatives, and that the Republicans only need to lose three seats to lose control of the House, it's not hard to see why forecasters are tipping a Democrat win.

If the midterms go as poorly for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, it could threaten Trump's command of the public's attention, as well as his authority over his party.

While he'll be in office for another two years, there's always an election around the corner in the US, and once the midterms are behind us attention will start to shift to the 2028 presidential election.

The results of these midterm elections will be an important moment in defining Trump's political legacy, as candidates start to position themselves for potential runs.

The current president regularly backs his preferred candidates in Republican primaries, and he believes his endorsement carries weight.

But will Republicans in the future be keen to embrace the Trump political project, or will they be keeping their distance the moment he's seen as a lame duck president?
news.summary: Donald Trump wants American voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot these midterm elections. Voters don't need to be reminded how much they dislike him.
news.author: Casey Briggs

news.title: Furious MAGA crowd turns on protester as Trump rally descends into chaos
news.text: A heckler was escorted out of Donald Trump's rally in Ohio as the US President faced yet another interruption during one of his speeches. A livestream of the event - used to garner support for the midterm elections next week - showed the man recording himself while shouting about Mr Trump and Jeffrey Epstein . The crowd of Mr Trump's supporters drowned out the man's heckling with "boos." This occurred as the man put up his middle finger and two security guards attempted to remove him from the stands. A male bystander helped security services as the disruptor appeared to resist and the three men moved the heckler out. The large crowd began chanting , "USA! USA! USA!" in support. The incident marks the third consecutive night that the US president's rally was disrupted by a heckler. The rally was the latest stop on Mr Trump's midterm campaign blitz to boost Republican candidates ahead of the high-stakes elections on Tuesday, November 3, which political analysts and polls suggest will be a bloodbath for the GOP. Earlier this week, one heckler shouted at the 80-year-old leader that he could "shove his ballroom up his a--", seemingly referring to Mr Trump's White House ballroom and East Wing renovation project, which is believed to cost around $600 million. Mr Trump called the heckler a "paid protester" but did not cite evidence. Later in the evening, the Ohio rally man, who appears to go by Robby Roadsteamer, posted his own phone footage of the incident on his X account. He appears to be a MAGA provocateur. It appeared that he was trying to remind the audience in Chillicothe, Ohio, that Mr Trump's name appeared repeatedly in the Epstein files following the bipartisan push to release legal documents connected to the convicted criminal - and Mr Trump's former mate. A mention or appearances in the files does not imply any wrongdoing. Mr Trump never been charged with any criminal activity connected to the late paedophile and sex offender and fiercely denies any wrongdoing. "Singing The Epstein Plane to Trump at his rally tonite! The raw footage. With the cops pulling me out! (Uncut)," he wrote in a post on X, attaching an over minute-long video clip. "Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane," the man began yelling in a deep voice. He repeated himself before getting drowned out in boos. However, he continued repeating the statement. His phone eventually dropped to the ground and he could be heard saying, "Ok, calm down." He picks the phone up and says, "Ow! No political violence! No political violence! No political violence!" as he is escorted out of the venue. An officer appears to tell the man that he was "uninvited" from the event, prompting him to ask, "Why? I'm singing hit songs! No, I wanna go back! We're having fun!" The officers continued to walk him out.
news.summary: The crowd of Donald Trump's supporters drowned out the man's heckling with "boos" in the latest disruption to the US president's rallies ahead of the midterm elections next week
news.author: Tannur Anders

news.title: Barack Obama and Donald Trump's Georgia Rally Crowd Sizes Compared: Photos
news.text: President Donald Trump and former President Barack Obama held rallies in Georgia just days apart, backing opposing candidates in two closely watched midterm races in the battleground state. Trump rallied at Guardian Centers in Perry on Saturday to support Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and U.S. Senate candidate Mike Collins. Obama joined Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms at a rally in Morrow on Wednesday. Photos and videos from the two events offer a glimpse of the crowds who turned out to hear Trump and Obama make their cases ahead of Election Day, as the two traded jabs over each other's leadership. Obama's Georgia Rally Obama joined Ossoff and Bottoms on Wednesday as Democrats sought to mobilize supporters ahead of the midterm elections. Promoted as the United for Georgia Rally, the event was part of the Democrats' effort to boost turnout in two competitive statewide races. In his remarks, Obama took aim at Trump over rising costs and accused him of launching an “unnecessary” war in Iran. He also criticized Trump's White House renovations. “He is spending time supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office,” Obama said. “He is literally doing arts and crafts while we are fighting a war and trying to deal with out-of-control prices.” Obama made similar comments at a rally in Michigan on Saturday for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, saying Trump has “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Trump responded to the remarks on Monday during a campaign stop in Mississippi, defending his decor choices and saying the White House “represents our country, and has to be pristine.” “I would try and explain that to a guy like Obama, but he wouldn't understand,” Trump said. “He doesn't understand the White House has to be clean, pristine, beautiful. It can't have cracks in the column.” Trump's Georgia Rally Trump held his rally on Saturday as he campaigned for Jackson and Collins, who are seeking to win the governorship and unseat Ossoff, respectively. During the event, Trump criticized Obama's stop in Michigan earlier that day, claiming the crowd had been small. “You know, I saw Barack Hussein Obama was in Michigan and the place was empty,” Trump told the crowd. “And they were saying, ‘Oh, this is a large crowd coming, the people are trickling through’—they don't talk about my crowds, they never talk about them.” What the Photos Show Photos from Obama's rally showed supporters gathered inside The Arena at Southlake in Morrow. The venue has seating for 8,000 people, according to its official website, though its capacity does not indicate how many attended Wednesday. At Trump's rally in Perry on Saturday, photographs showed supporters filling the seating area. Seats were full more than an hour before Trump took the stage, and a couple hundred people stood behind them, according to The Mercer Cluster, Mercer's student newspaper. FOX 5 Atlanta also described the event as packed, but venue officials had not released an official attendance estimate. Newsweek has contacted Guardian Centers and The Arena at Southlake for attendance estimates. Neither rally had a verified final attendance figure available in the sources reviewed. While photos and local reporting provide some insight into turnout at both events, they do not establish which rally drew the larger crowd. Georgia Polling The rallies came as Georgia voters prepared to decide competitive races for governor and the U.S. Senate. RealClearPolitics' polling average showed Ossoff leading Collins by 8.2 percentage points, at 51.2 percent to 43 percent. The latest poll included in the average, conducted by Quantus Insights from October 15 to 17, found Ossoff leading 52 percent to 45 percent among 755 likely voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. An earlier poll of 1,000 likely Georgia voters conducted by the University of Georgia's School of Public and International Affairs for The Atlanta Journal-Constitution from October 7 and 15 found Ossoff leading Collins, 48 percent to 40 percent, with nearly 12 percent undecided. The poll had a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points. The same AJC poll found the gubernatorial race between Bottoms and Jackson within the poll's margin of error, with Jackson receiving 46 percent support and Bottoms 45 percent. Eight percent of likely voters remained undecided. Georgia's record-breaking in-person early voting turnout continued Wednesday, with more than 2,203,600 voters casting ballots statewide as of Wednesday evening, according to the Georgia Secretary of State's Office. Early voting continues in Georgia through Friday. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.summary: The current and former presidents rallied in the battleground state just days apart in the final stretch before Election Day.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: A US cruise ship suspends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
news.text: SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia: A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said. .Those on the ship had hoped to sail for years to comePassengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”The company could not immediately be contacted for comment. .For some, the venture was a risk worth takingYet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end,” Larson said.Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. “You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over.”Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said..The cruise began in Northern Ireland in 2024The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Trump Unravels After Protester’s Epstein Plane Taunt
news.text:
President Donald Trump had a meltdown after a protester interrupted his rally by yelling about his flights on convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s “Lolita Express.”

Trump, 80, was belaboring his anecdote about admiring GOP incumbent Sen. Jon Husted’s “a--” at a rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, Wednesday night when a protester seized the moment during the president’s brief absence from the microphone.

“Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane!” the man yelled from the stands, prompting event security to drag him out of the venue as the crowd erupted into boos.

The protester identified himself as Rob Potylo, a musical comedian and political activist known as “Robby Roadsteamer.” 

Potylo, who dresses in a giraffe costume and uploads anti-Trump parody songs on YouTube, was arrested by federal agents in January during an ICE protest in Minneapolis, Boston.com reported. He was also detained by ICE in Portland, Oregon, in October 2005, the report added. He told Boston.com that he went to Minneapolis to “see what I could do to sort of help the cause and bring my art to the darkest areas.”

On Wednesday, he shared his point of view on the heckling in an Instagram video and an “uncut” version on X. He wasn’t in his usual giraffe onesie; instead, he wore a pro-Trump hat.

“Just got Trump in Chillicothe Ohio!,” he wrote on his X page. “Sang The Epstein Plane song, called him ‘Pumpkin Spice Peeedo’ and gave him the finger then got attacked!”

Potylo was referring to one of his YouTube videos, titled, Jeffrey Epstein Plane.

He added, “I’m okay I think! I do it for you!”

Trump responded on stage with a jab, saying he was “paid” and “not a young guy,” before another protester on the opposite side of the gymnasium disrupted him again.

Trump’s crowd of supporters responded with scattered chants of “USA” before the president reclaimed the spotlight, taking the opportunity to comment on the first protester’s Epstein remarks.

“You know, he mentioned Epstein. So I threw Jeffrey Epstein out of the club like 20 years ago because I thought he was a whackjob,” Trump began. “That was a great thing I did, I must say.”

He continued, “And he never came up with me. You know who he came up with? All of the friends of the Democrats. He was a Democrat.”

Trump was also a Democrat 20 years ago. He registered as a Democrat in 2001 and remained affiliated with the party until September 2009, when he returned to the Republican Party.

“And whenever they bring his name, you know, like the guy who was the head of Harvard who can’t—who got thrown off the board,” Trump rambled, seemingly referring to former Treasury Secretary and former Harvard University President Larry Summers. “No, I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-A-Lago.”

He continued, “And I was the one who was completely exonerated from him, but, uh, you know, they use it because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”

As the president devolved into more claims that his opposition was “paid,” a third protester interrupted him once again, flipping him the bird on her way out.

Reached for comment, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the Daily Beast in a statement: “Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him.”

Trump has repeatedly claimed he was not involved in any misconduct during his public relationship with Epstein, who was convicted of soliciting prostitution of a minor and later jailed on federal sex trafficking charges before his death by suicide.

Following the release of the federal government’s Epstein files, the president claimed he was “100% exonerated” and told reporters the DOJ had “announced” that he had “nothing to do with” the late sex offender.

The DOJ did no such thing. Trump appears in more than 5,300 documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, according to The New York Times.

One email released under the EFTA revealed that Trump was listed as a passenger on Epstein’s private plane, nicknamed the “Lolita Express” due to its infamous transport of alleged sex trafficking victims, at least eight times between 1993 and 1996.

“Donald Trump traveled on Epstein’s private jet many more times than previously has been reported (or that we were aware),” the email, written by an assistant U.S. attorney in January 2020, read.

In 2024, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he had “never on Epstein’s Plane.”

The president has a fondness for the word “exonerated,” however, using it publicly at least 10 other times to describe situations in which he was not, in fact, officially cleared of guilt in any capacity, as MS NOW reported in February.

Trump, 80, was belaboring his anecdote about admiring GOP incumbent Sen. Jon Husted’s “a--” at a rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, Wednesday night when a protester seized the moment during the president’s brief absence from the microphone.

“Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane!” the man yelled from the stands, prompting event security to drag him out of the venue as the crowd erupted into boos.

news.title: What Happens to Your Portfolio if the Stock Market Crashes? There's Good and Bad News for Investors.
news.text:
There isn't one strict way to define a stock market crash, but it happens when equities tank suddenly without warning. When living through them, it can feel like the world is ending. This feeling is exacerbated by investor panic or an economic shock.

The most recent started in February 2025, when President Donald Trump introduced sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. Before that, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in February and March of 2020 rattled markets. They're not common. But when they do take place, they surprise investors. And sentiment takes a massive hit.

What happens to your portfolio during a stock market crash? Investors need to look at both the positive and negative aspects to be fully prepared if such a scenario arises.

Equity prices will fall

It's no shock that during a crash, many of the stocks that you own will lose value. This could be a short-term phenomenon. However, it might also take a while for certain positions to fully recover.

Not all stocks will behave similarly. It all depends on the kinds of companies you have in your portfolio.

High-quality businesses should generally hold up better. Companies like this generate steady revenue that doesn't fluctuate too much with broader macroeconomic trends, as customers should still need their products and services regardless of the backdrop. Their profits and free cash flows are robust. And their balance sheets are in solid shape.

This doesn't mean that their share prices won't fall. They could still drop with the overall market, or with the sector that's getting hit hardest. However, these companies should still have relatively strong underlying fundamentals.

Unprofitable growth stocks are a different story. They typically need access to outside funding to keep operating. During a market or economic downturn, that funding can quickly dry up. As a result, these businesses face heightened uncertainty. And investors will become extremely pessimistic about their prospects.

These kinds of stocks are usually valued based on price-to-sales ratios. Shareholders should expect their valuation multiples to collapse.

You also have to think about market sentiment in this bleak environment. Negative headlines get all the attention. This can trigger a spiraling feedback loop. Falling stock prices can push even the most level-headed investors into a panic, leading to mistakes. And they might sell their stocks at the worst possible time in an effort to stop the pain, adding further downward pressure.

Downturns can present opportunities

Market crashes also come with some good news. The best investors know this is true. And they stay the course.

History shows that the market always recovers. The S&P 500 index has produced a positive total return in 94% of rolling 10-year periods since the 1930s. That stellar track record speaks for itself. And it suggests that crashes are blips on the radar if you zoom out.

Investing early and often and spending time in the market is profoundly more impactful than trying to actively jump in and out of positions. This trading mentality requires successfully figuring out when exactly to sell and when to buy back in again. That's a losing game that should be avoided.

Another positive development is that crashes present discount opportunities, as investors send both good and struggling stocks lower. Investors who adopt a dollar-cost-averaging approach -- consistently adding money to their portfolios each month regardless of broader market swings -- will see those allocations go further, enabling the purchase of securities at attractive valuations and introducing upside when equities bounce back.

"Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful," Warren Buffett wrote in an opinion piece in The New York Times during the financial crisis in 2008. To actually put these words into practice requires preparation. Besides being mentally and emotionally ready, investors have to have the cash on hand to play offense. This can turn crashes into opportunities.
news.summary: A clear-eyed look at both the pros and cons is essential.
news.author: Neil Patel

news.title: FTC orders Walmart, Delta and others to share how they use personal data to set prices and pay
news.text: The U.S. Federal Trade Commission said Wednesday it is ordering Delta Air Lines, Walmart and other companies to provide detailed information on how they use consumers' data when they're setting prices.The commission said it is also studying how ride-sharing and delivery companies like Uber use their independent drivers' personal data when setting compensation rates."We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service," FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.Orders were also issued to United, JetBlue, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart and Target, the FTC said.Each company must share information that will allow the commission to assess whether pricing for tickets, rides, food delivery or other products and services varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data, the agency said.The FTC said it is also examining whether companies compensate workers based on personal data like their phone usage or their history of accepting rides or deliveries. If the companies fail to turn over data, the FTC said it could compel compliance in federal court.Delta said in response that it has "zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing" and fully complies with pricing and advertising laws."There is no fare product Delta has ever used, is testing or plans to use that targets customers with individualized offers based on personal data," the company said in a statement.JetBlue said it doesn't use personal information or web-browsing history to set individual prices."Fares are determined by demand and seat availability, and all customers have access to the same fares," the company said.Instacart said compensation for its shoppers is based solely on job-related criteria, including the distance traveled, the number of items and expected shopping time. The grocery delivery company said it also doesn't use consumers' personal information to set prices. Prices on Instacart's website are set by the retailers the company serves."We appreciate the FTC's focus on this practice. We are committed to transparency and improving affordability for customers," a spokesperson for Instacart said Wednesday. "We will continue engaging with policymakers and regulators to ensure they understand how pricing on our platform works."Walmart's CEO said in a statement last month that the retailer doesn't use personal information like income, shopping history or a customer's willingness to pay to set prices, and it won't be doing so in the future either. Target also said in a recent post on its website that it doesn't use personal information to raise prices for customers "based on who they are, where they live or when they shop."The FTC's actions reflect customers' increasing concerns about pricing technology and the use of artificial intelligence to collect vast amounts of data. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing-related bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.In August, the FTC announced a proposed policy that would require businesses to "clearly and conspicuously disclose" if they are engaging in personalized pricing and share the types of data they're using to set those prices. The agency has extended the comment period on that policy until Nov. 21.In a preliminary report filed in January 2025, the FTC found that grocers, clothing companies and others were using third-party companies to help them individualize online prices based on shoppers' locations, browsing histories and other factors, including how long they left items in their virtual shopping carts.But Ferguson, who assumed the chairmanship of the FTC when President Donald Trump took office, has said that report was rushed and should have asked the companies directly for data instead of focusing on third-party intermediaries.
news.summary: "We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service," FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.
news.author: Aplast Updated

news.title: Piers Morgan takes aim at Trump's fired Katie Zacharia press secretary - 'cut the c***'
news.text: Piers Morgan has accused President Donald Trump 's short-lived press secretary of being a pro-Trump 'robot', despite being sacked just five days into the job. news.title: Trump rallies Ohio voters behind Vivek Ramaswamy
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 29 (IANS) US President Donald Trump urged Ohio voters to elect Vivek Ramaswamy as governor, bringing the Republican nominee onto the stage at a campaign rally where Ramaswamy promised property-tax relief and action against sanctuary cities. Addressing supporters in Chillicothe six days before the midterm elections on Wednesday (local time), Trump predicted a Republican victory and repeatedly appealed for voters to support Ramaswamy and the party’s congressional candidates. “Six days from now, the people of Ohio are going to elect Vivek Ramaswamy as your governor,” Trump said, according to the supplied rally transcript. The president later invited Ramaswamy to address the crowd, giving him another opportunity to set out his economic and immigration message in the closing stretch of the campaign against Democrat Amy Acton. Ramaswamy framed the contest around which candidate would improve voters’ lives, explicitly linking his state-level promises to Trump’s national agenda. “President Trump puts Americans first,” he said. “I'm going to put Ohioans first.” He pledged what he described as the biggest property-tax relief package in Ohio’s history if elected. He did not provide figures, a financing plan or a legislative timetable for that proposal in the remarks. Ramaswamy also promised to end sanctuary cities in Ohio, presenting the commitment as a state-level extension of the administration’s immigration policies. In his earlier address to the rally, he said he would act by executive order on his first day in office. Both commitments were campaign promises. The speech did not announce an enacted tax measure or a new state immigration order. Trump repeatedly returned to the importance of turnout, telling supporters they could not take victory for granted. His endorsement was part of a wider appeal to elect Republicans across the ballot and preserve the party’s ability to advance his agenda in Washington. The president also defended Ramaswamy against criticism of his campaign, accusing the media of treating him unfairly. He attacked Acton’s record and political positions, while Ramaswamy criticised her handling of the state’s response to Covid. Trump combined his appeals for Ohio candidates with a renewed promise to give adult US citizens $5,000 each if Republicans won both the House of Representatives and the Senate. “If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate, I am going to give all adult citizens in the United States $5,000,” he said. He described the proposed payment as a dividend, put its cost at approximately $1 trillion and said recipients should spend the money inside the United States. He did not set out a payment schedule or detailed funding mechanism at the rally. The president also promoted tariffs and domestic manufacturing, arguing that his trade policies encouraged companies to produce in America. Those claims formed part of his broader campaign argument that Republican victories would protect jobs and household incomes. Ramaswamy closed his appearance by urging supporters to vote and expressing confidence that the party would win. Trump repeated his appeal for the candidate near the conclusion of the event. Ramaswamy and Acton are contesting Ohio’s governorship in the November 3 elections. The Chillicothe event brought the state race together with Trump’s campaign for Republican congressional candidates, allowing the gubernatorial nominee to present his priorities directly to the president’s supporters.

news.title: JD Vance targets visa fraud, worker replacement
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 29 (IANS) US Vice President J.D. Vance said President Donald Trump had empowered him to tackle visa fraud and challenge employers replacing American workers with lower-paid foreign employees, making job protection a central theme of a campaign speech in North Carolina. Speaking at a midterm election rally in Kinston, Vance linked visa enforcement to the administration's broader argument that government should prioritise American workers and domestic investment. He did not announce a new visa policy, identify a fresh enforcement action or specify changes to eligibility, application procedures or employer obligations. His remarks described the administration's priorities rather than a newly issued rule. "The President has empowered me and the team to cut down on visa fraud and fight against anybody who would lay off an American worker and replace them with a low-wage foreigner," Vance said. He added that "American jobs ought to go to American citizens". Vance did not identify the team he was referring to or explain when Trump had given him that responsibility. He also did not name any employer accused of misconduct, present evidence of a particular violation or announce penalties against a company. The passage contained no reference to India, Indian workers or the H-1B programme. It did not distinguish between temporary work visas and pathways to permanent residence. The vice president returned to employment near the end of his speech, promising support for businesses that invested in American workers while warning those moving jobs overseas. "I want to send a message to the business community that if you're willing to work with us and invest in American workers, we are going to be your biggest champion," he said. "But if you want to ship American jobs overseas, then we are going to fight you tooth and nail because American jobs ought to go to American workers." He framed both arguments around national sovereignty, saying elected leaders should answer to American citizens and protect the livelihoods of people working in agriculture, manufacturing and the armed forces. Vance criticised earlier political leaders for encouraging production overseas, arguing that communities such as the Ohio town where he grew up had been neglected. Those comments formed part of his campaign case for maintaining Republican power in Washington. He recalled his grandfather's work as a union welder at a steel mill in Middletown, Ohio, and described the pride his grandfather took in vehicles made with American steel. The vice president also tied his employment message to household aspirations, including owning a home, raising a family and securing dignified work. He urged voters to support Republican candidates whom he portrayed as more committed to those goals. His visa remarks were part of a broader rally address covering immigration, public safety, taxation and manufacturing. The speech supplied no timetable for further visa-related announcements and no details of individual investigations. Kinston is in eastern North Carolina, where Vance recalled serving as a Marine at nearby Cherry Point. He opened the address with memories of military life and the support he received from the surrounding community. The rally took place six days before the November 3 midterm elections. Vance urged supporters to turn out with friends and relatives, backing Republican candidates and seeking the return of Representatives Greg Murphy and Richard Hudson to Washington.
