news.title: Trump floats plans of naming Hormuz Strait into Trump Strait again
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 29. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has again said he would like to rename the Strait of Hormuz the Trump Strait.

"I think we're going to rename [the Strait of Hormuz] the Trump Strait . Well, we named a Gulf known the Gulf of Mexico into the Gulf of America. We're going to name that the Trump Strait at some point," he said, addressing a GOP rally in Ohio ahead of the midterms.

"We have a gulf. We have a lake. We might have a strait. We might do that. You think I'm kidding? You know, they thought that I was kidding when I named the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. Oh, that's so funny! No, I said I'm going to do it," the US leader added.

According to Trump, more oil is currently flowing out of the waterway "that it was seven months." After the conflict with Iran ends, he continued, "the price of gasoline and the price of oil is going to go."

Earlier, the American leader signed executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario as the Gulf of America and Lake America, respectively. However, Trump’s successors as president could sign executive orders reversing these changes.
news.summary: The US leader also added that more oil is currently flowing out of the waterway "that it was seven months"

news.title: Iran keeps diplomacy open as US weighs fresh strikes
news.text:
Araghchi says ‘in contact’ with mediators after Qatar presents new seven-day plan to end war• US warns Gulf states of possible ‘short, intense’ Iran war after midterms, reports WSJ

TEHRAN: Iran’s foreign minister said on Wednesday that Teh-ran remained in close contact with mediators over ways to impl-e-ment its proposal to end the Middle East war, even as Iranian officials rejected ideas put forward by Qatar for a new agreement.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran continued to give diplomacy a chance to succeed and raised the possibility of the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran being completed in less than a week if implemented.

Araghchi’s remarks came as Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said.

The official briefed on the negotiations, who is not from Iran, said a new draft peace proposal for the eight-month-old conflict was presented on Sunday and was being considered by Tehran, with a response expected by the end of the week.

Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and recently spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran’s and Washington’s concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.

The draft discussed in Tehran on Sunday was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. The official had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.

US military preparations

Meanwhile, the US has told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a “short, intense military campaign” against Iran after the Nov 3 midterm elections, Anadolu reported, citing The Wall Street Journal.

The messages, conveyed through diplomatic and military channels, are among growing signs that the US and Israel are preparing a new round of heavy combat operations to wea-ken Iran and push it toward negotiations, according to the report.

Washington is moving a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to the region and has moved troops from bases where they were vulnerable, while US forces are restocking munitions and preparing bombers and fighter jets for strikes, the newspaper said, citing officials.

An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit are expected to join roughly 20 US warships in the Middle East next month, it added.

US President Donald Trump has not made a final decision, but is leaning toward a “large postelection attack” that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, the report said, citing people familiar with his thinking.

US war costs top $47bn

The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25 per cent higher than the Defence Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.

The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29bn to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.

More than $6bn would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft, including many drones lost during the war.

news.title: Obama Mocks Trump’s ‘Arts and Crafts’ as US Fights War, Prices Rise
news.text: Former President Barack Obama mocked President Donald Trump for “literally doing arts and crafts” in the Oval Office as he criticized the administration over war and high prices during a campaign rally in Morrow, Georgia, on Wednesday. Obama delivered the remarks while campaigning for a pair of Democrats, U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms in the final days before Tuesday's midterm elections. Ossoff is defending his Senate seat against Republican Representative Mike Collins, while Bottoms is running against Republican Rick Jackson for governor. During an extended attack on Trump’s priorities, Obama turned to the president’s changes to the White House and the gold decorations he has added to the Oval Office. “I’m not making this up, the president of the United States is spending time supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office,” Obama told the crowd. “He’s literally doing arts and crafts while we are fighting a war and trying to deal with out-of-control prices.” “The administration’s own actions are directly responsible for rising costs,” Obama said. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions, the most important of which was to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for.” Obama repeatedly returned to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and rising prices as he made his case against Trump and Republicans in the final days of the midterm campaign. Obama Revives Cheesecake Factory Feud Obama’s “arts and crafts” attack came as he revisited his mockery of Trump’s White House renovations, which sparked days of pushback from the president and his administration. At a rally in Ohio over the weekend, Obama said that Trump had made the White House look “like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Trump subsequently defended his renovations and criticized Obama, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent visited a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, D.C., and used the appearance to hit back at the former president. On Wednesday, Obama suggested the scale of the Trump administration’s reaction proved his broader point about its priorities. “Let me get this on the record. I am the father of two daughters,” Obama said. “Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory? That was my jam.” Obama argued that the administration had not disputed his criticism over prices or his accusations of corruption but had instead focused on his restaurant remark. “The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison. That part didn’t bother him,” Obama said. “But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comments. He took great umbrage.” “They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke,” he continued. “Not to inflation, but to that joke.” Obama singled out Bessent’s appearance outside the restaurant, noting that the Treasury secretary is responsible for economic policy. The former president then joked about his own experience dealing with the financial crisis after taking office in 2009. “I inherited this major financial crisis. I never called my Treasury secretary and said, ‘You’ve got to go to Arby’s. Order roast beef. No cheese though, that may look elitist,’” Obama said. “This is what I mean when I say these are not serious people,” he added. “They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.” Obama Hits Trump Over Iran and Putin Obama also criticized the Trump administration’s foreign policy, contrasting the current conflict with Iran with his own approach to Tehran’s nuclear program. “We had curbed their nuclear program,” Obama said. “I had put in place a deal. I didn’t have to fire any missiles. I engaged in diplomacy.” He also accused the White House of surrendering to the demands of strongman Russian President Vladimir Putin and “selling out” Ukrainians. “The White House is bending the knee to Vladimir Putin of Russia,” Obama said, “and selling out Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom and democracy.” On the economy, Obama portrayed Trump as having failed to deliver on promises he made before returning to the White House. “I’m a fact guy. So let’s play back the tape,” Obama said. “People heard Trump promise to get costs under control.” Obama cited Trump’s promises on tariffs, foreign wars and healthcare before telling the crowd: “If you thought everything cost too much before, guess what? Everything is more expensive now.” Obama Campaigns for Georgia Democrats Obama’s appearance came as Democrats made a final push to support Ossoff and Bottoms ahead of Election Day. The former president also took aim at Trump more personally, accusing him of aiming to enrich himself and his family, comparing the behavior to that of foreign "dictators." “He is very much focused on enriching himself and his family,” Obama said. “That’s what dictators in other countries do. But that’s not what we do.” Obama later recalled the controversy during his own presidency over his decision to wear a tan suit. “I am old enough to remember when a president wearing a tan suit was a major national controversy,” Obama said. “They were very upset.” “And I know I looked good in that suit.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Obama mocked Trump for doing “arts and crafts” as he criticized the president over war, rising prices and White House renovations.

news.title: Trump orders talks on machinery imports
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 29 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has ordered negotiations with trading partners over imports of robotics, industrial machinery and their components, citing national security concerns while leaving open the possibility of future tariffs and other restrictions. The proclamation directs the Commerce Secretary and the US Trade Representative to jointly pursue or continue negotiations and provide a progress update within 180 days. It does not impose an immediate new tariff or specify a rate for the products covered. Trump accepted the Commerce Secretary's finding that the quantity and circumstances of these imports threatened to impair US national security. According to the proclamation, the secretary submitted a report on the investigation within the preceding 90 days. "Depending on the status or outcome of such negotiations, I may consider alternative remedies in the future," Trump said in the proclamation on Wednesday (local time). Those options include imposing or modifying tariffs, duties, quotas and fees. Trump also raised the possibility of a programme to encourage investment in US production of robotics, industrial machinery and their parts and components. The directive leaves the selection of negotiating partners to the Commerce Secretary and the trade representative. It does not name India or announce a country-specific agreement, exemption or restriction. The officials must keep Trump informed about the status or outcome of the talks, with at least one update required within the 180-day period. The proclamation does not say that tariffs will automatically take effect when that period ends. Commerce must also continue monitoring imports and reviewing their implications for national security. The secretary is required to alert the president to circumstances that could warrant further action. It also describes military applications for advanced robots, including reconnaissance, casualty extraction and mine detection and clearance. Automated manufacturing helps defence producers increase output, including during war or other armed conflict, according to the document. The Commerce Secretary found that the United States depended on foreign supplies for most types of robotics, industrial machinery and related components. Imports had increased in value over the past decade and were projected to rise further, the proclamation said. The secretary also identified potential cybersecurity risks from equipment supplied by certain foreign entities. Such machinery can be integrated into manufacturing and defence systems that process and store sensitive information, according to the findings summarised in the proclamation. Despite increased investment in US manufacturing facilities, domestic output remained below consumption and capacity was insufficient to meet national security needs, the document said. It also cited underused manufacturing capacity within the sector. A separate White House fact sheet presented the negotiations as part of an effort to strengthen domestic production and reduce dependence on imported equipment. Neither that statement nor the proclamation announced a completed deal or quantified new investment resulting from Wednesday's action.

news.title: US DOJ is inquiring about Nvidia's purchase of Hugging Face
news.text: The US Department of Justice has made inquiries about how Nvidia's $12.93 billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face would affect competition in artificial intelligence, at the same time as antitrust enforcers pursue their years-long investigation into the chip designer's conduct, two people familiar with the matter said.The Justice Department's recent questioning covers Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, the two people said. On Hugging Face, Justice Department officials have asked whether the deal would let Nvidia capture a fundamental distribution point for AI, the people said. The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2027, Nvidia has said, adding that Hugging Face would continue to support work with a range of chip, cloud and AI providers.The department's questions around the Hugging Face deal and details of its continued pursuit of Nvidia's conduct more broadly are reported for the first time here. Nvidia has become a cornerstone of the tech economy and AI boom, backing major players such as Anthropic and OpenAI while spurring data center development globally so its chips can power AI's voracious computing needs.Any action by the DOJ could ripple through the chip industry and challenge Nvidia's investing and acquisition strategy that has extended its influence in AI. Government investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and do not necessarily result in lawsuits.A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on any matters before the department, citing longstanding policy. The spokesperson added, "This DOJ under President Trump's leadership will continue to prioritize advancement of Super Intelligence for the betterment of the American people."Nvidia declined to comment, and Hugging Face representatives did not respond to a request for comment.The broad Nvidia examination started under former Democratic President Joe Biden and has continued under the administration of Republican President Donald Trump, during which time Nvidia has been the most valuable company in the world and a singular force in AI. There is no indication that Trump has any involvement, and the probe may not result in any Justice Department action.As part of the probe, the DOJ has examined Nvidia's acquisition of SchedMD, one of the people said. The December 2025 purchase sparked worries among AI specialists about their access to SchedMD's open-source software, which helps run supercomputers relevant to national security. Nvidia has vowed to continue open access and support.NVIDIA AND TRUMPNvidia has the biggest share of the market for AI chips, which power the likes of ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and similar tools. A host of startups and chip-design companies have challenged its dominance.Competitors Broadcom and Alphabet's Google design processors together, seeking to beat Nvidia hardware with chips purpose-built for specific tasks and AI software. Advanced Micro Devices has said it can produce technically superior hardware and has struck billion-dollar deals with several AI labs and cloud computing operators.Nvidia's market position has nonetheless made it an industry force and helped CEO Jensen Huang develop a relationship with Trump, who has touted American AI. Huang and Trump have made frequent appearances together, with the CEO joining the president's diplomatic trip to China. Trump, who has disclosed owning Nvidia stock, separately awarded Huang the National Medal of Science for advancing AI hardware.Trump critics have previously accused the administration of political intervention at the DOJ, which the administration has disputed. Such intervention is traditionally out of the ordinary.Staff-led investigations at the DOJ often take years and can stretch from one administration to the next. In addition, the DOJ routinely seeks input from companies when evaluating proposed mergers. "It would be inappropriate for the Department to conduct a merger investigation under the guise of a conduct investigation," the DOJ spokesperson said.SCRUTINY OF OTHER NVIDIA DEALSThe DOJ has scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its 2025 deal to license technology from chip startup Groq and hire its engineers, the people said. Officials have explored whether Nvidia unfairly offered larger allocations of AI chips if customers purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, raising questions about whether Nvidia used its dominant product to push into a newer market, the people said.Nvidia declined to comment, and Groq did not respond to a request for comment.The DOJ has also looked at Nvidia's acquisition of Run:ai, which makes software that helps AI chips run more efficiently, the people said.The department's questions about the proposed Hugging Face acquisition include identifying how Nvidia might use the AI platform to harm rivals in the AI market, and whether Nvidia could use the newly acquired business to gain leverage, the people said.Officials are also asking questions about Hugging Face's competitors, said the people.
news.summary: The Justice Department's recent questioning covers Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, the two people said.

news.title: Trump shelters Flávio Bolsonaro, risking tensions with Brazil
news.text:
The US decision to allow the defeated right-wing Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro to seek refuge in the US poses a fresh irritant to a bilateral relationship that has been marked by finger-pointing and accusations between the two countries’ leaders.

The United States issued visas for Bolsonaro and his family as US President Donald Trump continued to criticise the election that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won last weekend. The relationship has already been marked by rancour, too, as when Lula warned at the United Nations General Assembly last month that other countries should not “undermine popular will.”

Trump said he would allow Bolsonaro to come to the US because Brazil’s election was “terrible” and “rigged” – and because he knows the candidate’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, “very well.” The elder Bolsonaro, a Trump ally during his time as president from 2019 to 2023, is serving a 27-year sentence for his role in plotting a coup attempt after the 2022 election to prevent Lula from taking office.

“Some of Lula’s willingness to work with Washington will be informed by how Trump deals with this right now,” said Nick Zimmerman, former director for Brazil and Southern Cone Affairs at the White House National Security Council. “It’s too soon to be confident that there’s disaster, or that things will get better. The dust needs to settle.”

For the time being, Lula may not have much to fear. Trump seemed to put a little distance between him and Bolsonaro’s refuge in Florida.

“I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we’ll see,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. “But I won’t get involved. It was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”

Trump last year hit Brazil with tariffs in an attempt to halt a criminal case against Jair Bolsonaro – a bid that only rallied Brazilian public support for Lula.

Lula is looking to the Trump administration’s next moves before assessing the effect on relations between the two countries, according to a person close to the Brazilian president.

That assessment will depend on whether Trump receives Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo for meetings in Washington, the level of support his administration extends to the defeated candidate, and the outcome of the US midterm elections next week, the person said.

Lula continues to favour a pragmatic, diplomatic relationship with Washington and is keeping plans to travel to the US for the Group of 20 leaders’ summit in December at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Miami, the person said.

Trump and Lula appeared to patch things up late last year at a summit in Malaysia, and Lula visited the White House in May. Yet tensions flared again in recent months. Brazil blocked visas for two senior US State Department officials over concerns that they wanted to cast doubt on the country’s electronic voting system before the election. The State Department later denied that was the purpose of the officials’ trip to Brazil.

Lula’s administration over the summer refused to give diplomatic approval to Trump’s ambassadorial pick, saying that it wanted to wait until after the election. The US in turn said it would revoke the visa for Brazil’s ambassador.

Trump’s welcome may provide Bolsonaro, who faces who faces at least two federal investigations in Brazil over allegations of money-laundering, with a platform for his grievances about the election. On Wednesday, he declared that he would lead opposition to Lula from the US and alleged electoral fraud, without providing evidence.

Yet Brazil’s courts view the election as a settled matter, and Lula has been recognised by almost all governments in the region – even those led by ideological opponents like Colombia. The Trump administration also wants to work with Brazil in areas like energy and critical minerals development.

Bolsonaro’s exile in the US may come to little, if his father’s experience is any guide. After disputing his loss in the 2022 election and alleging that voting machines were rigged, Jair Bolsonaro, too, flew to Florida just before Lula’s inauguration, staying for three months before returning to Brazil where he was placed under arrest.

“President Trump famously does not like a loser, and Flávio’s own allies have walked away from him in Brazil,” said Ricardo Zuniga, a longtime foreign service officer who served in Brazil. “It’s hard to see how an extended conflict between the White House and the Lula administration makes much sense for the rest of Trump’s agenda.”

by Eric Martin, Bloomberg
news.summary:
Decision to take in Flávio Bolsonaro will affect bilateral relations; Lula said to be looking to the Trump administration’s next moves before assessing the effect on relations between the two countries.

news.title: Dutch PM Says Europe Won’t Return to Russian Gas Amid US Peace Talks
news.text:
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten sharply rejected the idea of restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe as part of a potential US-brokered peace agreement with Moscow, calling it a “very stupid idea” and urging Washington to increase sanctions rather than offer economic concessions.

Speaking alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky in The Hague on Wednesday, Oct. 28, Jetten responded to reports that US negotiators had floated the possibility of reviving Russian energy exports to Europe as part of a broader settlement to end the war in Ukraine.

“It is clear that we need to push Putin to take the negotiations seriously,” Jetten said, arguing that Russia was suffering mounting military losses and economic pressure from international sanctions.

“The only way forward for Europeans, but also for Americans and others, is to put more sanctions on the Russian regime instead of less,” he said.

“So buying Russian energy is a very stupid idea,” Jetten added.

The Dutch leader said Europe had demonstrated since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine that it could substantially reduce its dependence on Russian fossil fuels.

“I can assure you that there is no European leader willing to buy Russian gas in the next few years,” he said.

Jetten insisted that economic pressure should continue until Moscow ends its invasion.

“What we want is Russia to stop this war, and as long as they don’t, we will hit them hard in their pockets with sanctions.”

US explores restoring energy ties with Russia

Jetten’s remarks come amid reports that Washington is exploring renewed energy cooperation with Moscow as part of negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.

As Kyiv Post reported Wednesday, citing the Financial Times, US and Russian officials have discussed the possible return of American energy companies to Russia, including joint oil production projects on Sakhalin and renewed Russian crude exports to Europe through the Druzhba pipeline.

Other proposals reportedly include restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe and potentially reviving the Nord Stream pipeline system.

The reported discussions involve economic incentives that Moscow could receive under a peace settlement, although no final agreements have been announced.

US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have been involved in negotiations with Russian and Ukrainian officials.

Europe has already moved to ban Russian gas

The European Union adopted binding legislation in January 2026 to permanently phase out Russian natural gas imports.

Under the timetable, long-term Russian liquefied natural gas contracts are to end from January 2027, with remaining pipeline imports phased out by November 2027 at the latest.

The measures form part of the EU’s REPowerEU strategy, designed to eliminate dependence on Russian energy and prevent Moscow from using energy supplies as political leverage.

Russian gas has not entirely disappeared from the European market. Some EU countries continue receiving Russian liquefied natural gas under existing contracts, but the bloc has committed to ending those purchases.
news.summary: Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten rejected proposals to restore Russian gas supplies to Europe as part of a potential Ukraine peace settlement, calling the idea “very stupid.” His remarks followed reports that US negotiators were exploring economic deals with Moscow, including renewed energy cooperation. Jetten urged Washington and European governments to tighten sanctions rather than offer Russia economic concessions.

news.title: Pentagon’s watchdog refuses lawmakers’ request to probe Starshield issues in Ukraine — AP
news.text:
NEW YORK, October 29. /TASS/. The Pentagon inspector general has refused a request by a group of senators to look into recent disruptions to Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine, The Associated Press (AP) reported.

In a response obtained by the news agency, the Pentagon watchdog told the group of nine senators that "their concerns are better answered by the Air Force." The lawmakers viewed that as a refusal to investigate SpaceX founder Elon Musk, according to the Associated Press.

Earlier, Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire) said that she and eight other senators have sent a letter to the Department of Defense’s Inspector General, "calling for an investigation into the disruption of the US-maintained Starshield systems for Ukrainian partners." According to the bipartisan group, the above-mentioned government authority should "determine whether any US officials approved of or had advance knowledge of the disruptions in service."

In mid-October, Kiev said SpaceX had introduced restrictions on Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian troops at speeds above 160 km/h, disrupting a number of Ukrainian military operations. Musk, in turn, said the Starlink satellite system was not used for offensive military operations and served only defensive and civilian purposes. He said Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, which determines usage and speed restrictions through the military and, ultimately, the president. The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered the restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield.

On the evening of October 22, US President Donald Trump said Ukraine’s access to the Starshield military satellite communications system had been restored.

news.title: Preventing Atrocities
news.text:
Aarif Abraham

Never again” to genocide is one of the international community’s most brittle postwar promises, often invoked only after the killing has begun. Yet mass atrocities seldom arrive without warning. Attacks on the rule of law, discrimination, dehumanisation, and impunity for earlier crimes are familiar, easily discernible precursors. These signals are increasingly visible globally. We are witnessing the largest number of active armed conflicts since 1946.

Around one in five countries has recently dealt with a mass atrocity, and people in half the world’s countries say they experienced some form of mass atrocity in 2024. Only 6.6% of the world’s population now live in full democracies. War crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and aggression are becoming part of the international system’s operating environment. This troubling trend is being intensified by an illiberal convergence on the United Nations Security Council, where three of the five permanent members have, to varying degrees, challenged the postwar legal order and moved to weaken the institutions charged with interpreting and enforcing it. For the world’s middle powers—countries like Canada, Brazil, and Japan—this new reality is as much a practical concern as a moral one. Atrocity crimes drive human displacement, destabilize entire regions, disrupt markets, and demand costly responses.

The Institute for Economics & Peace’s Global Peace Index estimates that violence cost $21.8 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 18.5% of global GDP. No state can insulate itself from such disruptions, and the danger only grows when states target the institutions that seek to deliver accountability for human-rights abuses. Sanctions and political attacks directed at the International Criminal Court, for example, are not merely jurisdictional disputes. They strike at one of the few mechanisms capable of imposing legal consequences for atrocity crimes, making future atrocities more likely.

The recent accolades for South African jurist Navi Pillay, the recipient of this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, and the Anglo-French legal advocate Philippe Sands, who received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade, underscore the same point: accountability is an essential condition for durable peace and security. I write this having recently conducted an 18-month inquiry, alongside Baroness Helena Kennedy and other leading legal experts, that culminated in The Atrocity Crimes Review. Though our findings concern the United Kingdom, failure to act against atrocity crimes is not uniquely British.

Many governments have leverage (through diplomacy, intelligence, sanctions, and other economic channels), yet lack the machinery to turn warnings into consistent, accountable action. The UK has no cross-government strategy, ministerial mandate, or specified budget for atrocity prediction, prevention, and response, and many other democratic governments are similarly lax. Atrocity prevention is not conflict prevention by another name. Atrocities also occur in peacetime through detentions, forced labour, surveillance, persecution, and organised expulsions, all of which can in turn drive conflict.

Moreover, the warning signs, perpetrators, and policy responses differ. Mediation can end a conflict, but it will not necessarily stop an atrocity. When bad actors are preparing mass violence against civilians, the task is to deter, disrupt, and, where necessary, punish. The UK, as a middle power, does valuable accountability work. But its approach remains ad hoc and reactive.

In Ukraine, it has supported investigations, sanctions, and training since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. But the warnings were sounding before Russia’s 2014 seizure of Crimea. Even today, the UK lacks a process to assess atrocity-specific risks, escalate warnings, and coordinate action. This is a bureaucratic failure that creates legal and strategic risk. Under the Genocide Convention, a state’s duty to prevent arises when it learns, or should normally have learned, of a serious risk of genocide.

Discharging that duty requires assessing the situation, escalating when appropriate, and acting before it is too late. Governments may object that formalizing prevention would fetter foreign policy or constrain strategic relationships. But this is a false choice. A formal framework need not compel interventions or condemnations in every case. Rather, it would require consistent risk assessments, recorded decisions, and processes to preserve lawful options. Without a proper process, ministers may find themselves hostages to late crises, litigation, or public outrage.

The United States under President Donald Trump offers a cautionary lesson. The US was the only state that had an advanced, actionable atrocity-prevention programme; now that it has been largely dismantled, the global consequences have been dire. The fiscal case for a formal process is equally strong. Early warnings, specialist staff, civil-society partnerships, and rapid escalations cost a fraction of what it does to respond after atrocities destabilize regions or displace millions. The peace dividend from averting atrocities is measured in lives and economic costs, just as the defence dividend is measured by wars averted. What a credible strategy looks like is straightforward: appoint a responsible minister with coordinating functions; create an independent advisory body; preserve the specialists whom you might need on short notice; establish early-warning and escalation channels; engage with survivors and civil society; scrutinize sanctions, arms exports, and supply chains; and report to legislatures.

Finally, in seeking to prevent atrocities, states should also address aggression, since unlawful wars often enable other international crimes, as the second- and third-order effects from the wars in Ukraine and Iran show. No state can prevent every atrocity. But the world’s middle powers, acting collectively, can use Security Council seats, regional organisations, intelligence-sharing, sanctions, trade, and development partnerships to deter perpetrators, support accountability, and strengthen the rule of law. States can act diplomatically and lawfully before violence escalates, and defend international courts before harm becomes irreversible. As we witness another civilian bombing in Kyiv or unlawful attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, coordinated action by like-minded states has grown more urgent. “This isn’t a call for sentimentality,” former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown explains, “but a call for statecraft, so that the law becomes operational, not ornamental, and early warning leads to early action.” Atrocity prevention is a national-security, economic, and legal necessity. States that built the postwar legal order, including Britain, need to meet it head-on.

These signals are increasingly visible globally. […]

news.title: WATCH: Trump ally declares himself ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to US
news.text:
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has declared himself the rightful leader of his country after arriving in the US, having fled Brazil following his election defeat to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

Bolsonaro, an ally of US President Donald Trump, landed in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday morning aboard a private jet after traveling through Argentina and Ecuador. He defied a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports amid investigations into alleged financial crimes.

The senator is suspected of involvement in a money-laundering scheme linked to fraudulent deductions from pension payments. He also faces a separate investigation involving alleged financial misconduct. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing, describing the cases as politically motivated.

The right-wing senator narrowly lost to Lula, a veteran left-wing politician, in Sunday’s runoff election, despite receiving more votes than his rival in the first round on October 4. His father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election defeat to Lula. The elder Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing, arguing that the case was politically motivated.

In a lengthy letter posted on X, Flavio Bolsonaro described himself as “the leader of Brazil” and claimed that the election was rigged. An earlier version of the letter had described him as the country’s elected president.

“The illegitimate and illegal actions of Lula’s former lawyer allowed a mathematical impossibility to become reality, with Lula gaining more than 10 million votes between the first and second rounds,” he wrote.

Bolsonaro was referring to Supreme Federal Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, who previously represented Lula. Zanin ordered voting extended from 5pm to 7pm on Sunday following complaints from Lula’s campaign about public transport disruptions. The last-minute ruling caused confusion because some polling stations had already closed, prompting Zanin to clarify that the extension applied only where voting was still underway.

Bolsonaro provided no evidence of electoral fraud. Lula won the runoff by approximately 4.4 million votes, while just 34,393 ballots were cast after the original 5pm deadline, according to Brazil’s electoral authorities. The figure includes votes cast by people already waiting in line when polls were due to close.

Bolsonaro rejected the investigations against him and vowed to “lead the opposition” from abroad. “It was not my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading. This is the classic playbook of any coup d’état,” he wrote.

Lula earlier condemned Bolsonaro’s departure as “a shameful act,” arguing that “those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear.”

Trump has also suggested that Brazil’s election may have been rigged. He previously condemned the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch hunt” and called for the case against the former president to be dropped.
news.summary:
Flavio Bolsonaro has arrived in Miami after losing Brazil’s presidential election, alleging fraud and declaring himself the country’s leader

news.title: 3 Wall Street firms agree to pay up to $100,000 a month to get Trump’s posts faster
news.text: US President Donald Trump’s paid social media service, Truth API, has found customers, with Bloomberg and two high-frequency trading firms paying for faster access to his posts. The service costs financial institutions up to $100,000 a month.Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter, cited by Reuters, said Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading, both of which specialise in algorithmic and automated trading strategies, have also signed up for the service.The deals give subscribers a timing advantage over people who monitor Trump’s posts on the app themselves.The arrangement has raised concerns about the sale of faster access to statements by a sitting president, particularly because his posts can influence financial markets.It also comes as Trump Media and Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social, faces legal challenges over the paid service and questions about the potential use of presidential communications for commercial gain.How Truth API worksTrump Media and Technology Group announced the faster-access product in July, pitching it to trading firms and other financial institutions. The service is designed to deliver Trump’s posts more quickly than a person could obtain them by repeatedly checking Truth Social.Trump Media officials have put the timing advantage at 50 milliseconds. For financial firms using automated trading systems, that difference can matter when a presidential statement triggers a change in asset prices.High-frequency traders rely on software to scan news headlines, company announcements and government statements for information that could move markets. Their systems can read and analyse the information before executing trades in thousandths of a second.The potential consequences of Trump’s social media posts were evident in April, when oil futures fell after he announced a ceasefire in the Iran war on Truth Social.An application programming interface, or API, acts as a digital bridge that allows one computer system to communicate with another. In this case, the product gives subscribers faster access to the president’s posts, which they can use in their trading or financial information systems.Who is paying for the service?According to a Reuters report, Bloomberg, Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading are among the organisations that have signed up for Truth API.In August, Trump Media told investors it had "signed more than 10 customer agreements”. Reuters was unable to independently confirm that figure.The company did not identify its customers but said they were primarily Wall Street trading firms paying between $60,000 and $100,000 a month. The latest deals indicate that the product has attracted both financial trading firms and a news and data provider.Reuters, which competes with Bloomberg in financial news, said in a statement: "We will assess the service, but have no current plans to subscribe."Trump Media defended the product in a statement, saying: “Truth Social offers an industry-standard API product for which there is significant demand across industries. We take customer confidentiality seriously. This reporting is based on misleading information being peddled by anonymous sources aimed at harming our company, customers and shareholders.”The company has not publicly named the subscribers in its August investor update, and the three firms named in the report declined to comment.Why the paid feed has drawn criticismThe paid service has drawn criticism for giving subscribers faster access to a president’s statements, potentially offering financial firms an advantage when his posts move markets. The deals are likely the first time a business linked to a sitting president has sold access to his statements.In July, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the service violated securities laws. They called it a “shocking abuse” of office by a president seeking personal gain.A Trump Media and Technology Group spokesperson said, “Congressional Democrats continue to mischaracterize Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.”In August, Intercept Media and the non-profit Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump, seeking to stop the White House from posting official government announcements exclusively on Truth Social. The ongoing lawsuit describes the service as "profoundly corrupt" and alleges violations of the First and Fifth Amendments.Trump Media’s financial portfolioThe commercial arrangement has also drawn attention to the ownership of Trump Media. The president’s family trust owns 41% of the company, and Trump is the trust’s sole beneficiary.The Truth API deals come as Trump Media faces a steep decline in its stock market value.Shares of the company have fallen more than 50% so far this year. Its market value has also been volatile since it went public in March 2024.The company closed at a market value of about $8 billion on its debut in March 2024, but is now worth about $1.8 billion.Since 2024, Trump Media has lost about $1.76 billion, including non-cash charges.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Donald Trump's Truth API, a subscription-based social media service, is attracting a diverse clientele, including Bloomberg and various trading firms, by offering rapid access to his posts. This service's growing popularity raises ethical questions about the commercialization of presidential communication and its potential effects on market dynamics. Amid ongoing legal challenges and mounting criticism, Trump's media company faces heightened scrutiny due to its reduced market value and controversial business practices.

news.title: Obama says The Cheesecake Factory was his 'jam' — and that Trump was less offended by being compared to Saddam Hussein
news.text: Barack Obama wants to set the record straight: he loves The Cheesecake Factory as much as the next dad. The former president defended his record on the California-based restaurant chain while campaigning for Democrats in Atlanta on Wednesday. At a campaign rally in Cleveland on Saturday, Obama said President Donald Trump's White House renovations had it "looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory." The joke sparked dayslong backlash from Republicans and the White House, who framed Obama as an elitist out of touch with average Americans. Obama countered by saying he's spent plenty of time at the restaurant chain. "I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to The Cheesecake Factory?" Obama asked the crowd on Wednesday. "I lived at Chuck E. Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen and The Cheesecake Factory. That was my jam for about a decade." Following Obama's initial comment over the weekend, Trump called him a "lousy president" for comparing the White House to the restaurant. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ate at a Cheesecake Factory on Monday and said he "would tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try." Obama, who was campaigning with Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, criticized the response to his comment. He said the White House devoted more energy to rebutting his Cheesecake Factory joke than to addressing affordability or allegations of corruption. "The president wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison," he said. "That part didn't bother him, but he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory. He took great umbrage." Obama said the White House "mobilized" a response to his joke but "not to inflation," pointing to Bessent's Cheesecake Factory visit: "This is the man who is in charge of the economy, the person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable." The White House did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The Cheesecake Factory did not respond to a request for comment and has not publicly addressed the controversy. The company did, however, score a win on Tuesday, when it reported a third-quarter earnings beat. Its stock price was up over 100% this year as of market close Wednesday. Cheesecake Factory executives did not mention the controversy on the earnings call.
news.summary: Obama defended his Cheesecake Factory credentials after his joke about Trump's decor sparked backlash from Republicans and the White House.

news.title: Trump says Xi nuclear meeting 'maybe single most important', orders robotics import talks
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 29 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on nuclear disarmament was already scheduled and could be "the single most important meeting", as he ordered negotiations with trading partners on imports of robotics and industrial machinery. "We're meeting with, scheduled already with President Xi of China. And we have a meeting on nuclear disarmament… Maybe the single most important meeting," Trump told reporters at the White House on Wednesday (local time). "China's much further behind, but they'll catch us within five years," he said. On the Russia-Ukraine war, Trump said, "Well, we talked about Iran, talked about Russia. And I think with Russia, we're making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine. There'll be a meeting set up very soon, and I think a lot of progress is being made." Asked who would meet, he said, "With President Putin and President Zelensky." On Iran, Trump said, "With Iran, we're in a very good position… they want to make a deal, but they like tapping it along. Maybe they're waiting for the election or something, but that's not gonna help them." "We've decimated their military. We've decimated their finances. They have no money. They have inflation the highest in the world, 301 per cent a couple of days ago," he said. Asked whether there could be a surprise against Iran after the midterm elections, Trump said, "I can't tell you that… but anything's possible." Earlier, departing the White House, Trump was asked about Vice President JD Vance's role on Iran. "No. He asked me what I thought, and I said if you want to do that, that's OK," Trump said. Trump also attacked Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska. "Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be prosecuted criminally for what she did… That's voter fraud at the highest level," he said. He referred to a "fake Dan Sullivan" and said Peltola "should be taken off the ballot". Asked about visa issues involving the family of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, Trump said, "I thought they were treated very unfairly." Asked whether Flavio Bolsonaro was the rightful president, he said: "I'm not going to make a comment about that… It was a very strange election, that's for sure." Separately, Trump signed a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 on imports of robotics, industrial machinery and their parts and components. The proclamation said the Commerce Secretary had found that such goods "are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States." Rather than imposing immediate tariffs, Trump directed the Commerce Secretary and the US Trade Representative to "jointly pursue negotiations of agreements" with trading partners and to update him within 180 days. "Depending on the status or outcome of such negotiations, I may consider alternative remedies in the future, including imposing or modifying tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees," the proclamation said. It said robotics and industrial machinery supported "approximately $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024" and warned that such equipment "from certain foreign entities" can "pose significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities". The proclamation did not name any country. The action adds to a series of Section 232 investigations into strategic sectors that could eventually affect exporters worldwide, including those in India, which is negotiating a trade agreement with Washington.

news.title: Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots, says it would 'wreak havoc' on voting
news.text: A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens, warning it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.The ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state. Over 500,000 votes have already been counted.The Department of Justice appealed the decision Wednesday evening.The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term.EARLIER: The DOJ ordered California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizensThe Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.The federal government's request, Carter wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The federal government also had asked the appeals court for a quick ruling — before a district judge’s scheduled Oct. 27 hearing in the case — but that effort was rejected by the higher court.RELATED STORY | Appeals court declines to rule on federal bid to set aside California ballots of alleged noncitizensThe Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in Congress.Carter's order was a forceful rebuke of the federal government's demand, arguing that segregating ballots at this time in the election would require counties to develop new methods for sorting ballots and “risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters.” In other words, Carter argued, it would have the same effect as purging voters and therefore violates the National Voting Rights Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls within 90 days of an election.“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”Carter also rejected the Justice Department's argument that California was impeding the federal government's ability to enforce the law. He argued that prosecutors already demonstrated the ability to enforce election law when they arrested 28 noncitizens who had voted or registered to vote illegally.MIDTERMS | Trump in Ohio and Obama in Georgia make closing stretch appeals to midterm voters in pivotal statesFederal prosecutors did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment on Wednesday evening.First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who argued on behalf of the federal government on Tuesday, has previously said that the federal government’s request wouldn’t impede the election. Instead, he argued that the Justice Department was trying to “safeguard the elections.”“Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later,” he said. “It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots.”
news.summary: A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens.
