news.title: Worse off under Burnham: The middle-earners and families struggling with bills who face a fall in living standards under Labour's 'is that it?' Budget
news.text:
Worse off under Burnham: The middle-earners and families struggling with bills who face a fall in living standards under Labour's 'is that it?' Budget

Scroll down to meet the families grappling with Burnham's 'is that it?' Budget 

By JASON GROVES, POLITICAL EDITOR and JAKE HOLDEN, UK NEWS REPORTER and JOSHUA HAINING, NEWS REPORTER

Published: 00:01 GMT, 29 October 2026 | Updated: 02:12 GMT, 29 October 2026

John Healey faced a backlash last night after an underwhelming Budget that left families facing a fall in living standards.

The Chancellor pushed up taxes to a record high and poured billions of pounds more into benefits.

But he ducked tough decisions on increasing defence spending and curbing the runaway welfare budget.

And a package of measures designed to ease the cost of living was so modest it was last night dubbed the 'Gherkin Budget' after Mr Healey boasted of tariff cuts that will shave a few pence off a jar of pickled cucumbers.

In a withering assessment, Kemi Badenoch said the Budget 'does not come close to meeting the moment'.

The Tory leader said: 'We have overspent, over-borrowed, over-taxed and are drowning in an out-of-control welfare system.'

She added: 'Most people listening to this Budget will be thinking to themselves, is that it? Really, is that it? The Prime Minister came in promising to reverse 40 years of neo-liberalism. Instead, we got 4p off gherkins.'

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its anaemic growth forecast for next year to just 1 per cent.

But experts fear that the situation could get worse within days, as speculation mounts that Donald Trump is planning new bombing raids on Iran after next week's midterm elections in the US, which would drive oil prices higher still.

In his first Budget as Labour Chancellor, Mr Healey: 

Raised taxes on savers, landlords and banks as he continued the Labour Government's record of pushing up the tax burden to new highs at every Budget;

Offered a £100 rebate to 20million homes in council tax bands A to D to help offset soaring energy bills this winter;

Published official forecasts showing that inflation and government borrowing are both on course to rise;

Signed off an extra £5billion a year in welfare spending after failing to bring forward reforms;

Delayed a planned 6p-a-litre increase in fuel duty until July;

 Faced criticism after he set a target of spending three per cent of GDP on defence by the end of the decade – but failed to say how it would be funded;

 Bowed to pressure to scrap Rachel Reeves's plan to cut the tax-free cash Isa limit.

Mrs Badenoch accused Labour of kicking difficult decisions into the long grass 'because the Prime Minister wants to keep the option of an early election open – putting his party's interests before the country'.

Some Labour MPs were also speculating last night that the PM is preparing a snap election after weak growth forecasts for next year were downgraded again.

The Prime Minister said he could 'rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months'.

He insisted that the Budget did contain some 'bold' measures, including the council tax rebate to help offset energy bills, even though it is likely to be swallowed up by a jump of several hundred pounds in the energy price cap come January.

The PM said the package would make a 'significant' difference 'if you add it all up'. Mr Healey described the package as a 'Budget for working people'.

He said the measures would give people 'breathing space' from an energy crisis triggered by a war 'we did not want'. The Chancellor insisted he would 'bring down the welfare bill' in future.

But he said it would be done 'in a Labour way'.

He said he was committed to 'fiscal discipline' and pencilled in tough spending limits for the final years of the decade. Economists said unprotected departments such as the Home Office and transport could face real terms cuts of 2.6 per cent a year.

But he gave no indication of how the savings would be achieved.

Economist Paul Johnson, former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: 'The numbers add up because the numbers were made up. If business and the country need some certainty and stability to help with growth, this Budget did not provide it.'

The OBR warned that living standards are set to fall in the next 12 months. The watchdog's forecast for real household disposable income per person is now £420 lower than two years ago and is not predicted to recover until April 2029.

OBR economist David Miles said Britain was facing a 'pretty grim picture' for living standards, with real incomes no better than they were before the pandemic.

The centre-Left Resolution Foundation think-tank described the outlook for living standards as 'dire'. Chief executive Ruth Curtice said the Chancellor had 'spread the jam thin' and warned that his decision to cut the buffer against breaking his own fiscal rules meant he now 'doesn't have enough to survive one bad roll of the dice'.

The Chancellor said it was right to use some of the so-called headroom to help soften the impact of the 'global economic storm' caused by the Iran war.

But he faced criticism on all sides for his timid approach. Rain Newton-Smith, CBI chief executive, said: 'This Budget lacks the bold moves that would have made it easier for firms to invest, hire and grow.'

Andrea Egan, Left-wing leader of the Unison trade union, said: 'This was the Government's first chance to turn the Prime Minister's historic ambition for a new economic settlement into action. On that count it falls short.'

Overall, Mr Healey hiked taxes by £7billion a year, following on from the £66billion levied by Ms Reeves in Labour's first two Budgets. The OBR said the tax to GDP ratio would pass its historic high of 37.2 per cent next year and continue rising for the next five years. The Chancellor maintained the long-running freeze on tax thresholds, which have already dragged millions of people into higher tax bands.

Reform UK's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick described the Budget as 'an exercise in fiddling while the economy burns'.

Below, read the verdicts of the real people affected by the Budget. 

£100 off our energy bill 'won't help long term' 

Name Abigail Giles

Lives: Berkshire

Job: Teacher and influencer

Teacher Abigail Giles with her electrician husband and their daughter Millie

Berkshire mother-of-one Abigail Giles said there was still 'not a lot of help for working families' facing massive energy bills in the new year.

Her family – which also includes her daughter Millie, 3, and electrician husband James, 34 – will qualify for the £100 energy bill relief, but she says this 'doesn't really help out long term'

She said her 'energy bills through the winter before have been £200 in just a month', and this is likely to rise further as the energy price cap goes up – along with virtually all other costs of living.

The removal of the gas standing charge is not much help either as their home is mainly heated electrically.

Her husband James's van runs on diesel for his business JG Electrical, and despite the fuel duty freeze, she said, 'costs are really mounting up. We really think it's making everything harder and is just another high cost to consider.'

And Mrs Giles added of another increasing essential cost for households: 'I'm just sick of worrying about the mortgage rate. Ours, at the moment, is looking at going up £300 to £400 a month from November.'

Mrs Giles works as a teacher but has had to go part time and start a social media 'mumfluencer' page – abigailfinds.uk – to get freebie days out to entertain Millie which they otherwise 'couldn't afford' and help other families in the same position.

'It shouldn't be this hard to get by,' Mrs Giles said, 'I'm a teacher, James is an electrician, we're in quite good jobs. It shouldn't be that hard.'

 Business rates relief will make 'a big difference'

Name: Kyle Hyams

Based: Surbiton, southwest London

Job: Coffee and gelato shop owner 

Kyle Hyams, his wife and three daughters pictured together in one of his gelato shops

Kyle Hyams welcomes the small business rates relief announced in the Budget.

He said the threshold increase from £12,000 to £18,000 giving 70,000 smaller firms a tax break will make 'a big difference'.

He will now not be paying any business rates at his premises, which mainly comprise coffee and gelato shops across southwest London named after his daughters Aoife and Orla.

But he noted that many business owners won't feel the benefit.

He began making gelato in 2024 with the aim of growing it into a national brand, but his ambitions are hindered by high VAT payments and rising National Insurance and minimum wage.

'Despite huge calls from the hospitality industry to reduce VAT rates to 10 per cent, there was no mention of this, which I find disappointing,' he said.

While the announcement of a 3.9 per cent increase to the national minimum wage is great for employees, he said: 'This is another expense for business owners without the support needed to raise these funds.'

He also felt there could be more support with energy bills for businesses.

He said: 'Everything we're trying to do to grow is being hindered by the government and by the constant moving of goalposts.'

'No one wants to invest more when they're not guaranteed a return on it. I feel like they're [the government] sort of crushing the dreams of people who have got high aspirations for what they want to achieve.'

 'We are definitely going to lose customers'

Name: Jo Bevilacqua 

Based: Orton Longueville, Peterborough 

Job: Hair and beauty salon owner

Jo Bevilacqua, owner of Serenity Loves, an award-winning hair and beauty salon in Peterborough, said she will lose customers following the announcement of a 3.9 per cent increase to national minimum wage.

'It is going to put added pressure on us without a shadow of a doubt,' she said. 'We're going to have to put our prices up which will possibly outprice customers. We're definitely going to lose customers.'

Her business, which will turn 15 next March, has survived Covid, energy price shocks and the cost-of-living crisis.

Now the 42-year-old, who employs 16 staff including six apprentices, is faced with tackling a further minimum wage increase after a string of extra business taxes under Labour since 2024 including higher National Insurance.

'We're trying to invest in the next generation, but it is becoming increasingly difficult,' she said.

Jo Bevilacqua in her hair and beauty salon, Serenity Loves, in Peterborough

Training apprentices costs up to £15,000, and it takes four years before she sees a return on investment.

She feels young people are desperate to find meaningful employment, but businesses are not being given the means to help them.

'We had a paid six-week internship program last March, we had eight positions open and had 150 applicants.

'Young people want to work and get their foot in the door, but businesses cannot afford to take them on.'

She added that she was 'very underwhelmed' with the Chancellor's Budget, saying: 'They talk about backing businesses, but I don't see how they're doing that.

'They talk about supporting new entrepreneurs but what about the other businesses that are trading right now?'

'Why are we considering taxing British people for choosing to holiday in Britain?' 

Name: Amanda Stecker 

Based: London and Oxfordshire 

Job: Luxury holiday home letter

Amanda Stecker owns and lets out six luxury cottages in the Cotswolds, but was dismayed to hear the introduction of the overnight visitors tax.

It could mean tourists – including British holidaymakers – would have to pay 5 per cent tax on their overnight accommodation.

But it seems like a backwards way to support local economies, Mrs Stecker said: 'Why are we considering taxing British people for choosing to holiday in Britain? At our cottages, 70 per cent of guests are British.

'These are precisely the visitors who help keep local economies alive outside the peak tourist season.'

Luxury holiday home letter Amanda Stecker in front of one of her cottages in the Cotswolds

Mrs Stecker began her business, Unique Cotswold Cottages, with one cottage eight years ago – buying cottages, doing them up and then letting them out to tourists.

It has been a great success which has allowed her to expand to buy more cottages, but with rising costs, she is now having to postpone these plans.

She said: 'I'd love to grow it more, but at the moment, I just can't do so, because the margins are too tight to have enough to pull together to purchase another cottage.'

She explained where the extra costs had hit the business following hikes to the minimum wage and National Insurance contributions: 'Our housekeeping and laundry costs are going up by 17 per cent in December alone. That's just one of the many increases we're facing.

'We can't keep absorbing these costs, but neither can we endlessly increase prices for our guests.'

The renovation side of the business is also feeling the pinch as materials costs have shot up.

Mrs Stecker said: 'We're already being squeezed by rising operating costs, and now there's talk of another tax on our guests. At what point do we start supporting British tourism rather than making it more expensive?'

'It feels incredibly unfair' 

Name: Charlotte Owen

Lives: Pudsey, Leeds

Job: Freelance journalist

Charlotte Owen and her two children Harriet and Sebastian with her husband Alex

Mother of two Charlotte Owen said middle-income families are 'feeling the squeeze' as income tax thresholds remain frozen.

She said it 'feels incredibly unfair' that her husband Alex, 39, has just been 'tipped over' into a higher tax bracket in his new £54,000-a-year social care job he started in September.

'You get higher tax, higher student loan payment and you feel like you're back to square one.'

While the couple and their children Harriet, 3, and Sebastian, 5, do qualify for the £100 council tax relief, she said 'it will only go so far' while the cost of childcare, groceries and energy bills soar.

Meanwhile, the scrapping of the gas standing charge is only due to save her £6 a month, she said.

'They're not giving me any more money in my pocket or 'breathing space' as Healey suggested; they're just saying it's not going to be any more expensive until July'.

Her experience as a self-employed freelancer has made life that much more difficult too. 'If I can't work, I don't earn,' she said, 'and I don't feel like there's a lot of help for self-employed people.'

Mrs Owen said that for her and many other families in her position, parents often face a disincentive to work as more time on the clock means having to pay for more costly childcare.

She explained: 'If I were to be self-employed and freelance for five days a week, could I guarantee that would earn enough to send them both to after-school clubs or nursery for five days a week and have enough money to pay other bills that are my responsibility? I'm not sure.'

She said she and Alex had 'seriously thought about' having a third child, but sadly decided they could not afford to – 'We are already at our limit with two kids'.

 'I've voted Labour all my life' but they've left me 'absolutely shattered'

Name: Carrie Cox

Lives: Hove, East Sussex

Job: Florist 

Carrie Cox is a lifelong Labour voter but now feels 'absolutely shattered' and is reduced to tears by the burden placed on her beloved business.

The 62-year-old welcomed a halt in having to pay her business rates, but said: 'There is nothing in that Budget that actually is going to save the high street.'

She added: 'We're still squeezed from every direction with rising wages, employment costs, energy bills, rents, and making it increasingly difficult to keep the doors open.

'I think they go after small businesses because we're the easy touch, because we, on our own, we can't fight back.'

Fighting back tears, she worried for the future of her shop, Florian, in Hove.

She said: 'I've voted Labour all my life, and I think for the first time ever, I just feel absolutely shattered by it.'

To Mrs Cox, the increase to the minimum wage would not help young people in the working world as 'the cost is so minimally different to the living wage, and there are so many people that are trained who are looking for work.

Carrie Cox was in tears worrying over the future of her flower shop Floria in Hove, East Sussex

'You are better off employing somebody that's trained.' She said National Insurance contributions increases have meant that employers end up having to pay £16.50 an hour for those on minimum wage.

On top of this, Labour-run Brighton and Hove Council has decided to make her shop's street, Western Road, a red route, meaning cars are unable to stop at all.

She said this would ruin footfall, potentially removing at least 20 per cent of her shop's income.

'They are encouraging active farmers to give up.' 

 Name: James Bowditch

 Live: Bridport, West Dorset

 Job: Family dairy farmer

West Dorset dairy farmer James Bowditch said he was 'not overly surprised' the farming industry did not receive a mention in today's budget announcement.

'I wasn't expecting anything, I wasn't expecting a golden ticket at all,' he said. 'They are encouraging active farmers to give up.'

'They weren't trying to poke the bear because they know farmers can cause quite a lot of chaos in a short amount of time.'

Mr Bowditch, who owns 1,600 cattle across three farms totalling 1,500 acres alongside his family, added that inheritance tax, which failed to get a mention, is pushing the family away from farming.

'In a long-term plan I've got to start saving up for a £200,000 tax bill. I've got to future proof myself and hope they don't change the goal posts again,' he said.

'Every mayor gets some money, but every rural area doesn't get anything. We didn't get a mention. There's nothing for the farmer and nothing for the rural area.'

James Bowditch and his family pictured on his farm surrounded by cattle and his two dogs

Farms larger than 400 acres like his are vulnerable to more IHT due to Agricultural Property Relief.

But Mr Bowditch said there are not many viable commercial farms producing the nation's food under that size.

'They've gone after completely the wrong person. It feels like farmers actually producing food are getting both hands tied behind their backs. The rural economy is being paralysed.'

Although he never previously felt the need to protest, Mr Bowditch drove his tractor to London and took part in the 2024 and 2025 farmers protests. 

'Farmers don't like to be involved in politics, but we feel as though we are being drawn in,' he said.

I can't retire at 68 but I still think this is a 'compassionate' Budget

Name: Linda Southall

Lives: Cardiff

Job: Building site cleaner

WASPI Pensioner Linda Southall said the budget was 'compassionate' but has been unable to retire on her pension 

Pensioner Linda Southall will continue to face financial struggles but was able to describe John Healey's statement as a 'compassionate Labour budget for the people'.

She is unable to retire, picking up a 'brain-dead job' as a cleaner on a building site to make ends meet, and has had to sell her house in Cardiff and move to a cheaper one in Pembrokeshire.

She welcomed the income tax relief for the state pension, but a private pension of hers tips her over the edge, meaning she will have to pay £97 in tax.

But she will still overall be up £391 a year up after the 3.9 per cent increase to her state allowance starting in April.

Her private pension also means she is just £17 over the threshold for Pension Credit.

Mrs Southall was happy to hear tariffs on 100 supermarket products would be lifted to ease grocery costs too after having to live on discounted and tinned food.

She said: 'If I see a cheap offer, I'll just buy more beans, more peas, more whatever. So, I sort of forward plan that way. You shouldn't have to think of these things, but you do.'

'Any help from the government is appreciated by first-time buyers' 

Name: Layla Philips

Lives: Wymondham, Norfolk

Job: Works in local government 

Recent first-time buyer Layla Phillips feels that measures in the Budget will help others like her get their foot on the property ladder.

She bought her two-bed semi-detached home in Wymondham, near Norwich, with the help of the now scrapped lifetime Isa (LISA) in 2023.

The LISA will be replaced by the First Time Buyer Isa in April 2029 and the Your First Home scheme – an equity loan – announced in the Budget from next year.

Ms Phillips, 29, who purchased her property through shared ownership with a housing association, said the new scheme and Isa on offer were very different from the help she received.

'It's a completely different scheme they announced. With shared ownership I got a smaller mortgage of £62,000 and I pay rent on the remaining 75 per cent.'

She said the 20 per cent government equity loan could potentially work better but questioned whether it would be more affordable once the five-year interest-free period ends.

Layla Phillips outside her two bedroom semi detached new build home she bouth through the LISA scheme

Ms Phillips also welcomed the cut to the 25 per cent penalty on homeowners who purchased their first home through the LISA scheme.

'Scrapping the penalty would be a positive that has come out of the budget today,' she said. 'Any help from the government is appreciated by first time buyers.'

The cost of living is so high and the property market so competitive, becoming a first-time buyer is incredibly difficult, she added.

'There should be more affordable homes. With mine, there were only two properties under shared ownership and after one minute of the email notifying buyers that there was shared ownership they were gone.'

The mansion tax is 'lunacy'

Name: Francis Fulford

Lives: Great Fulford, Devon

Job: Businessman and TV personality

Francis Fulford was unhappy to hear no revision of the upcoming mansion tax on £2million homes.

He owns and lives in the manor on his family estate at Great Fulford in Devon. His family has lived there for over 800 years across 26 generations, but despite the grandiose appearance, Mr Fulford said: 'I'm not rich, I'm asset rich, but I'm not rich in terms of income.'

On hearing of the upcoming mansion tax that would levy an annual surcharge on properties worth £2million or more, he said simply: 'It's all lunacy.'

He argued that the tax has added to a plethora of recent policy against wealthy people in Britain – like taxing non-doms, the reduction of stamp duty thresholds and increasing levies on businesses.

'The mansion tax is yet another reason for them to f*** off,' Mr Fulford said, adding, 'It's GCSE economics, which, for some reason, nobody in the Labour Party or the Treasury seems to have ever done.'

Francis Fulford outside his manor on the Great Fulford estate which has been in his family for more than 800 years

His particular situation with Great Fulford also brought light to issues with how the law will be defined and implemented.

He said: 'We will argue that this house is valueless on its own.' This is because of the massive expense it takes to maintain – around £150,000 a year for the whole estate.

The value lies in the 250 acres of land surrounding it, he said, but questioned whether this would be included in the tax.

He added: 'If you put a tax on something, you immediately reduce the value,' further complicating which homes qualify.

He suggested that it would cut 'more than half a million' from the value of every property it is levied on 'because people will build into it in anticipation of that tax rising in the future'.

He added: 'The real danger with this particular tax is, like all taxes, they start low, but rise up,' and pointed to VAT starting at 10 per cent and now sitting at 20 per cent.

The war on landlords is 'marching us to the gates of hell' 

Name: Paul Jarvis

Lives: Stafford

Job: Landlord

Paul Jarvis said he is selling up his three properties after Labour levied an extra 2 per cent on his income from letting

Paul Jarvis says Labour's war on landlords is 'marching us to the gates of hell' and will 'cause a housing crisis' after the Budget announced income from properties was to be taxed an extra 2 per cent.

Following on from the additional 2 per cent previously levied by Labour, this means he will now have to pay 24 per cent income tax – rather than the standard 20 per cent basic rate – on the rent received from his three properties in Stafford.

Mr Jarvis has decided he will sell them all because 'it's too much hassle for what it's worth now'.

He said: 'I've had to put one of my rents up £150 a month, which I don't really like doing. Surely they can see that it's just been passed to the tenant. You're not gonna absorb everything.'

Mr Jarvis used to fit truck tyres in Birmingham, but after 19 years in the property business, he said he'd now prefer putting his money 'under the sofa'.

One of his three tenants has stopped paying rent for two months already, and other recent legislation could mean he loses out on more than a year of payments from the renter if the matter goes to court.

'It's literally every six months they're attacking landlords,' he said as he railed against the Renter's Rights Act, the landlord register and now this tax increase, labelling them 'just a money bank for the government'.

Mr Jarvis was desperate for these regulatory pressures to be reversed, but said in resignation: 'They ain't gonna help us are they?'

However, he was glad to see proposals of increases to capital gains tax dropped ahead of the sale of his houses.

A cut, not just a freeze, to fuel duty is 'absolutely necessary'

Name: Rhys Hackling

Job: Managing Director of Direct Connect Logistics

Rhys Hackling, managing director of Direct Connect Logistics, pictured with two lorries

Rhys Hackling said an actual cut to fuel duty rather than a mere freeze was 'absolutely necessary' for hauliers like himself.

The managing director of Bicester-based firm Direct Connect Logistics explained that following the fuel duty freeze, 'it still feels like we're being penalised'.

'We would have liked to see a reduction in the cost of diesel. For the public it's nice to have fuel reductions but for businesses like ours which are paying £24,000 more per month on fuel it's vital,' he said.

Since the start of the Ukraine-Russia war, diesel has risen more than 30 per cent at the pumps, having increased from around £1.30 to £1.90 per litre.

But Mr Hackling said hauliers don't have a choice about using diesel adding: 'There is no other form of fuel we can use.'

He issued a 'thank you' to the Chancellor for not increasing fuel duty, but said it was 'absolutely necessary' to go further.

He added: 'I would have also liked to have seen more about infrastructure in the Budget, but it was a little bit of a quiet Budget if I'm honest.'

Healey has launched yet another spiteful attack on the prudent – why I fear this is just the calm before the storm, says JEFF PRESTRIDGE

ANDREW NEIL: Labour believes in deficit reduction on the never-never. The more Healey talked of prudence, the more we noticed his profligacy...

news.title: Failed MAGA Mouthpiece Glitches as She’s Grilled on Trump
news.text:
Donald Trump’s flash-in-the-pan press secretary short-circuited when the president’s longtime frenemy put her in the hot seat.

Katie Zacharia, 41, lasted five days at the White House podium before her unceremonious exit. On Wednesday, she sat down with Piers Morgan, 61, for a showdown that grew testier by the minute. Ten minutes in, Morgan’s patience ran out.

“Come on, let’s cut the crap here and have a serious, genuine conversation,” the Uncensored host said. “You sounded like a robot. Has Donald Trump got some program plugged into you to make you come out with all this stuff?”

“I do not sound like a robot,” Zacharia shot back.

No White House press secretary has ever had a shorter run. Her debut briefing on Oct. 13 lasted 14 minutes and she fielded only three questions, including a gaffe where she accidentally called her husband “my president.”

Two days later, Fox’s Sean Hannity, 64, put her on the spot over the bar exam she failed and never retook. Within 24 hours, she was out.

Morgan opened with a jab, asking how it felt to be “in many people’s eyes a bit of a laughingstock.”

“Working for President Trump was an incredible gift,” Zacharia replied, describing it as a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

“Katie, he did fire you after five days,” Morgan said.

“Piers, this has been litigated and adjudicated,” she said. “The president’s comments on the White House South Lawn were what was discussed and I’m going to leave it there.”

Morgan played Trump’s remarks to reporters on the day he ousted her.

“I said, ‘Is this for you, Katie?’ Because honestly, you don’t need this,” the president said in part in the clip.

“I’m curious. Listen, I’ve known Donald Trump for 20 years... and I sort of understand the way he operates and the way he does things. In a very, very nice way, he was publicly chucking you under the bus there, wasn’t he?” said Morgan.

Morgan and Trump have been friends since 2008, when the president crowned him winner of The Celebrity Apprentice. Trump calls him “champ,” and Morgan has called Trump “a very loyal friend in many ways.” The bond has limits, though. Morgan insists he’s no MAGA supporter and slammed Trump’s AI video of the Obamas as “vile” and “racist.” 

Zacharia, meanwhile, dodged again. “As I said earlier, this has been litigated and adjudicated,” she responded, looking fed up.

“Why don’t you just answer some questions for me?” Morgan asked.

Zacharia repeated her answers and then changed the subject.

“Why aren’t we covering the first million barrels that arrived in Texas yesterday in his historic… 65 billion barrels of oil deal that he made with Venezuela?” she said, in part.. “Why aren’t we covering these [wins]?”

After more back-and-forth, Morgan asked, “You do realize you’re not the press secretary, right?”

He pressed her on what she told Trump when the president asked whether the job was for her. She refused to say.

“Piers, I will keep private conversations between the president and myself confidential,” Zacharia replied, as the host shot back, “he [Trump] made them public.”

Zacharia then put her foot down.

“I’m not gonna mince words or split hairs over this. I will not disclose private conversations that I’ve had with the president. I will keep fighting for him every single day. No matter how hard the media wants to spin, no matter how hard anchors, pundits, reporters, and journalists want to spin what he is doing and focus it on me. I will continue fighting for him. I am ruthlessly loyal. I always have been, and I will continue to be, Piers. This interview should not be about me; it should be about the fact that we are less than five days away from the midterms…”

“Katie, Katie, Katie, Katie, the whole point of the interview was it was about you,” Morgan cut in, before accusing her of being a robot, asking, “Has Donald Trump got some program plugged into you to make you come out with all this stuff?”

Zacharia retorted, “I take issue with the way you’re couching this...” she said, adding, “I do not sound like a robot to your point. What I am is trying to continue a conversation in a forward trajectory about what President Trump is doing, which you are not wanting to engage in...” She continued talking about serving the president “in the best of my capacity,” becoming increasingly heated.

Morgan, stopping her, repeated his position before Zacharia fired back that she didn’t receive the talking points from Morgan’s team. 

“What did you think you were going to be talking about? Morgan said, appearing baffled.

“Midterms. And a brief glance at my time as press secretary,” she said in the awkward moment.

After offering her the chance to provide the “brief glance,” Morgan twisted the knife. “We both got hired by Donald Trump,” he said. “The only difference is I never got fired by him.”

Zacharia accused Morgan of baiting her but claimed, “I’m not going to do it. I haven’t done it to this point and I’m not going to now. The focus should be on President Trump, not on me.”

“I haven’t asked you to say anything negative about him at all,” Morgan replied.

“Piers, you’re baiting me. I had the opportunity to serve him in the capacity that I was asked to. And I’m not going to go for it, and I’m not going to speak negatively of him. He’s been wonderful to me, and I’m grateful for the,” Zacharia said.

“I’m not baiting you,” a shocked Piers responded.

“You’ve been at the center of a gigantic news story because you became the shortest-serving press secretary in the history of the American White House. It made you a global figure, and you agreed to come on this show. 

“I’ve just checked with my producers exactly what you agreed to talk about is going to be you and what happened and their midterms. We haven’t misled you or misled anybody else. I’m not here to trap you. I’m just here to talk to somebody who was in the news who I’ve never met.”

He added, “I don’t know you, and I’m just curious about how it all felt. You don’t have to leave Donald Trump out of it if you like. I don’t care. Right? It was all just what happened to you. When you watch back, for example, the clips from your first and only press conference, what do you feel when you watch that?”

Zacharia, frozen, appeared unimpressed: “Piers, I am grateful to be here. I am not going to continue litigating this. This is over 10 days ago that this happened. We’re five days away from a midterm. I’m here on a show. What was told to me was going to be a brief overview of my time as press secretary and then discussing the midterms. I - that is what I agreed to come on the show, and I’m not going to continue having the focus be on me, Piers. I am not.”

“You’ve literally refused to say a single thing about it,” Piers shot back. 

Zacharia then pointed to her post-firing media tour, insisting she’d already said her piece. 

“As I said... the Wall Street Journal encompasses a lot of the questions you’ve asked. I wrote an op-ed in the New York Post, and I discussed this on my interview with Rob Finnerty last night on Newsmax.”

Later in the interview, Zacharia finally softened when Morgan asked about her family. 

She explained that relatives who had shunned her in 2020 were rallying behind her, saying they were “disgusted by the treatment of me.” Even her Democrat mother, she said, called to tell her “CNN was even more compassionate than some other networks.”

Morgan credited her with opening up. “You finally got uncensored, Katie,” he said. “Took a while, but there I started to see the real you.” If she’d sounded “less robotic” at the podium, he added, “I think you’d still be standing there.”

The Daily Beast has reached out to a representative for Zacharia for comment.

Piers Morgan uncensoredDonald Trump’s flash-in-the-pan press secretary short-circuited when the president’s longtime frenemy put her in the hot seat.

Katie Zacharia, 41, lasted five days at the White House podium before her unceremonious exit. On Wednesday, she sat down with Piers Morgan, 61, for a showdown that grew testier by the minute. Ten minutes in, Morgan’s patience ran out.

“Come on, let’s cut the crap here and have a serious, genuine conversation,” the Uncensored host said. “You sounded like a robot. Has Donald Trump got some program plugged into you to make you come out with all this stuff?”

news.title: Obama Blitzes Trump With Massive Crowd in Major Humiliation
news.text:
The tiny crowd at Donald Trump’s latest rally has been brutally compared to the much larger turnout Barack Obama enjoyed that same night.

Trump, 80, has been frantically touring America in an attempt to secure votes for the Republican Party next week, including two rallies in one day in Texas on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, Trump headed to Ohio to support his man-crush Sen. Jon Husted and embattled Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor. He selected the Shoemaker Center, an indoor athletic facility inside Ohio University’s Chillicothe campus.

The venue’s website said it has bleacher seating which can accommodate “approximately 2,400 spectators.” A damning photograph posted on X by NBC News Chief White House Correspondent Garrett Haake showed how small his chosen rally venue was.

“I’ve covered dozens if not hundreds of Trump rallies, and I can’t recall him ever holding one in a room as small as this arena in Chillicothe, Ohio,” Haake posted. “It’ll be packed, and loud-but maybe 1,000 people will fit.”

A photo posted by USA Today reporter Jessie Balmert from the rear of the venue, behind the elevated media platform, showed how compact the room was.

At the same time, Barack Obama headlined a campaign rally near Atlanta, Georgia, supporting the MAGA boogeyman Jon Ossoff, who is running for re-election to the Senate, and Keisha Lance-Bottoms, the Democrat running for governor of Georgia. The rally was held at The Arena at Southlake in Morrow, Georgia. The venue’s website lists its capacity at 8,000.

Footage and photos from the event showed the arena was at capacity, with more than three times as many people as Trump’s rally as even the upper seats were clearly filled.

Photos from outside the venue showed thousands of people lined up to enter the arena—something Trump often claims is occurring at his rallies, even as empty seats are clearly visible while he speaks.

On Wednesday, Ossoff introduced Obama, who came on stage to U2’s “City of Blinding Lights,” which was his signature walk-on song during his presidency. U2 members Bono and The Edge performed the song at the opening of his Presidential Center in Chicago in June this year. 

After a wild reception from the audience, which he said made him “fired up,” Obama stated his experience in politics meant, “You can tell when an election comes along, that just feels a little different. An election where people are so ready for something new...everywhere you go, it feels like change is in the air.”

Trump’s previous rally in Ohio, on October 12, was held at the Covelli Center, which can accommodate up to 7,000 people. However, only around 3,000 people attended that rally, according to estimates by the Tribune Chronicle.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Despite the small capacity, Trump made a bizarre comment on Wednesday about the popularity of his rallies, claiming “every rally” was “totally sold out, with thousands of people that can’t get in.” Trump has previously referenced viewing screens erected outside venues for people unable to get inside.

The senior president then appeared to flash back over a decade, talking about how the media covered Bernie Sanders compared to him.

“I have 42,000 people, ‘Donald Trump showed up’,” Trump said, referring to how the media reported on him. “Bernie Sanders had 312 people, we counted ‘em. ‘Bernie Sanders had a very active crowd, tremendous crowd.’ I have 42,000 people, they refuse to acknowledge it.”

That figure appears to refer to a rally in Mobile, Alabama, in August 2015, which his team said drew 42,000 people. However, police and fire officials estimated the crowd at around 20,000.

Trump’s rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, on Tuesday was also slammed for its low capacity. Breck Worsham, a former Trump supporter who claimed that she once worked on Trump’s campaign, stated, “He’s gone from selling out football stadium-sized venues to high school gyms.”

Trump, 80, has been frantically touring America in an attempt to secure votes for the Republican Party next week, including two rallies in one day in Texas on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, Trump headed to Ohio to support his man-crush Sen. Jon Husted and embattled Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor. He selected the Shoemaker Center, an indoor athletic facility inside Ohio University’s Chillicothe campus.

 92-year-old US judge handling Maduro case dies 







NEW YORK, United States (AFP) — Alvin Hellerstein, the United States (US) judge overseeing the case against deposed Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, has died aged 92, an official said Wednesday.

As one of the oldest US federal judges, questions had been raised about whether he was the right justice to preside over what could be a prolonged trial for Maduro on drug trafficking charges.

Hellerstein’s lengthy career included overseeing the civil cases arising from Al-Qaeda’s September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on New York and Washington, often rejecting deals he saw as unfair to complainants.

His death was confirmed by the United States District Court, Southern District of New York, where he presided. A court filing showed the case has been reassigned to Analisa Torres, born in 1959.

Hellerstein also tangled with Donald Trump, rejecting a request by the US president to have his New York hush money case moved to federal court.

Last year, he blocked the Trump administration from deporting alleged Venezuelan gang members without a court hearing.

In a noteworthy 2015 ruling, Hellerstein ordered the US government to release a trove of photos depicting abuse of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan.

He also presided over a trial last year in which a jury found French banking giant BNP Paribas’s work in Sudan had helped prop up the regime of former ruler Omar al-Bashir, awarding $20.75 million in damages to three plaintiffs from Sudan.

Hellerstein handled the sprawling drug trafficking case linked to Maduro for over a decade, which has already seen the conviction of Venezuela’s former intelligence chief, Hugo Armando Carvajal.

Maduro was seized by US forces in January in a military raid on his compound in Venezuela.

A graduate of Columbia University Law School, Hellerstein served as a lawyer in the US Army from 1957 to 1960 before entering private practice.

He was nominated by then-President Bill Clinton in 1998 to be a district court judge for the Southern District of New York.

news.title: Iran warns of 'devastating' economic fallout from any new Israeli attack
news.text: TEHRAN: Iran warned on Wednesday of a devastating economic impact from any new Israeli-led attack, as the votes were counted in an Israeli election that could determine the future of the regional war.The Islamic republic also said it was discussing with mediators ways to implement a seven-day plan to end the West Asia conflict and reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz.Under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has vowed to topple Iran's government, the two countries have directly fought a war for the first time in their history after decades of enmity.Tuesday's pivotal election gave Israelis a chance to offer a verdict on Netanyahu's right-wing government, amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran following their launch of the war in February."Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to recent discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow.Since the war erupted, it has severely disrupted energy shipments from Gulf countries after Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.Iran has restricted passage and regularly attacks vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation.In retaliation, the United States has been maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports, seeking to squeeze the country's economy.On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington had told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.But the newspaper, citing people briefed on the conversations, said President Donald Trump had not made a final decision..US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after midterm elections.Give diplomacy a chance Araghchi said on Wednesday that Iran was discussing a plan with mediators to end the war and reopen the strait."While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," he said in a post on X."We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week.". Trump had previously rejected the plan, after Iran proposed it in September.Araghchi had said at the time that under the plan, Hormuz would reopen within seven days if "necessary conditions", including a ceasefire across the Middle East, were met.Iran had also demanded the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector, and an end to the US naval blockade.Negotiations between Washington and Tehran have been stalled for months.US news website Axios reported on Wednesday that regional mediators led by Qatar were pushing for "a diplomatic deal" to restart US-Iran talks and prevent the resumption of war after the US midterm elections.The report, citing US, Israeli and other regional sources, said the Qataris were trying "to convince Iran to allow UN inspectors to visit its bombed nuclear sites in return for some sanctions relief from the US".Iran said a Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Sunday for talks..Existential threat Netanyahu, vying to form a coalition government after Tuesday's closely contested polls, has said Israel has an opportunity to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.His main electoral rival Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, has warned Israel's security top brass that they must serve the national interests and not the political needs of Netanyahu."Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.On Sunday, Israel's Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu and Israeli military chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir had clashed over an order for unspecified military action that defence officials feared could trigger renewed fighting with Iran.Netanyahu denied the report.As the votes were counted on Wednesday in the election, no clear winner had emerged between Netanyahu's bloc and an opposition camp led by Eisenkot.Tehran has said the outcome of the polls "makes no difference".On Sunday, Araghchi said a resumption of war with the US and Israel would also not change Iran's position."They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past," he said.Iran's military meanwhile has warned it would retaliate more widely against any new attack, with security chief Mohsen Rezaei saying it could strike US-related infrastructure including data centres and other artificial intelligence targets.Tehran has dismissed Netanyahu's threats to topple the Iranian government, calling them "empty" and "a sign of desperation"..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Before Alaska's Two Dan Sullivans, JFK Had Two Joe Russos
news.text: The controversy surrounding two candidates named Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race has an unexpected historical parallel: John F. Kennedy's first congressional campaign, when two men named Joe Russo ran against him in the 1946 Democratic primary. The Trump administration has sued to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that voters could confuse him with another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The lawsuit has drawn a response from Alaskan officials, who are asking a federal judge to dismiss the case. The November 3 contest could help determine control of the Senate. Eighty years earlier, Kennedy's campaign faced a similar name problem in Massachusetts. One of his opponents was a well-known Boston city councilor named Joseph Russo. The other was a 27-year-old janitor with the same name who entered the race under circumstances that later prompted allegations of political maneuvering. The episode offers a glimpse into Kennedy's early political career and a historical parallel to the dispute over the two Sullivans in Alaska. The Two Joe Russos in JFK's First Campaign In 1946, Kennedy was seeking the Democratic nomination for Massachusetts' 11th Congressional District, which included Boston's West End, North End and East Boston, as well as Cambridge, Somerville, Brighton and Charlestown. A Navy veteran from a wealthy political family, Kennedy was running for office for the first time. Among his nine primary opponents was Joseph Russo, an Italian immigrant who had become a prominent figure in Boston politics. Russo had arrived in Boston from Sicily with his family when he was 8 years old. He later established a funeral home and won election to the Boston City Council in 1938. By the time he entered the congressional race, he had served four terms and had a following among Italian American voters. Russo questioned Kennedy's qualifications, describing the Harvard-educated political newcomer as a "young squirt" and criticizing the advantages that came with his family's wealth. He also took a swipe at Kennedy's campaign in an advertisement that read: "Congress seat for sale. No experience necessary. Applicant must live in New York or Florida. Only millionaires need apply." But Russo faced an unusual complication: another Joe Russo was also on the ballot. According to the West End Museum, the second Russo was a 27-year-old janitor who was paid by Kennedy campaign manager Joseph Kane to enter the race, potentially confusing voters and splitting support for the more established candidate. The museum's account says Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., JFK's father and a wealthy businessman who later served as U.S. ambassador to Britain, reportedly approved the tactic, although it remains unclear whether JFK himself knew about it. A PBS American Experience documentary provides another account of the alleged arrangement. Mark Dalton, who worked on Kennedy's campaign, recalled that Joseph Kennedy and people around him had arranged for a second Joseph Russo to enter the race. Dalton said he had no doubt the man was paid to allow his name to appear on the ballot. "There's no doubt in my mind that Joe Kennedy and the people around him put one of those Joseph Russos in the fight," Dalton said in the documentary transcript. The allegations were not simply a matter of two candidates sharing a name. In a 1964 oral history interview preserved by the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, the elder Russo recalled facing multiple candidates with the same name in political contests. He said he had to advertise himself as the "Middle Russo" when other Joseph Russos appeared alongside him. What Happened When the Votes Were Counted The second Russo reportedly acknowledged that people had encouraged him to enter the congressional primary in exchange for favors. According to the West End Museum, he told a reporter that he had been offered assistance with housing and other benefits. Kennedy won the nomination in a landslide regardless, garnering 22,183 votes, compared with 5,661 for the city councilor and 773 for the janitor, according to the museum's historical account. The future Democratic icon went on to win the general election and begin his career in Congress. He would later serve in the Senate before winning the presidency in 1960. The elder Russo continued in public service after losing to Kennedy. Boston Mayor John Hynes appointed him to the city's Election Commission in 1949, and he later became its chairman. Russo did not appear to hold a lasting grudge against Kennedy. The museum recounts that the two encountered each other at the 1956 Democratic National Convention. Russo later told his children with pride that the future president had once been a candidate against their father. Alaska's Two Sullivans Face a Court Fight The current dispute in Alaska involves Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg who says he is running independently. Republicans have accused the challenger of trying to siphon votes from the incumbent, but he has denied being a political plant. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. should remain on the ballot. Election officials distinguish the two candidates by identifying the senator as a Republican incumbent and listing the challenger under his full name without a party affiliation. The state's ranked-choice voting system allows voters to rank both candidates. The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on October 22, seeking to prevent certification if the incumbent loses and votes cast for the other Sullivan could have changed the result. President Donald Trump has said he directed the department to bring the case. On Tuesday, Alaskan officials urged a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the federal government lacks a legal basis to intervene in the state's election certification process. They also questioned how officials could determine whether voters intended to select one Sullivan rather than the other without compromising ballot secrecy. A ruling could come before Election Day. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told Newsweek that even if the Peltola campaign encouraged Daniel J. Sullivan to run, that would not automatically make him ineligible or provide grounds to force Peltola out of the race. The two U.S. political episodes are separated by nearly eight decades, and the circumstances are not identical. Historical accounts describe an alleged effort to use a second candidate with the same name to divide support for one of Kennedy's opponents. In Alaska, the dispute raises a different question: whether the presence of a similarly named candidate warrants federal intervention in an election's certification. Both cases illustrate how candidates with similar names can become a source of controversy in American elections, while underscoring the distinction between allegations of political maneuvering and the legal standards governing who can run for office. news.summary: A dispute over two Dan Sullivans echoes JFK's 1946 congressional race, when two Joe Russos appeared on the ballot.

news.title: JD Vance Sends Letter to Iran Hard-Liner in Bid to Revive Peace Talks
news.text: Washington, DC: US Vice President JD Vance has opened a direct channel to one of Iran’s most powerful hard-liners in an attempt to revive peace negotiations, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. This development unfolds while US President Donald Trump threatens to resume military strikes in the approaching weeks.Vance transmitted a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, who serves as secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and is a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). This outreach was designed to examine whether Washington and Tehran might establish a framework for negotiations.According to a single individual acquainted with the subject cited by the WSJ, the letter was dispatched at Trump’s direction, and the president remains fully informed regarding the initiative.In a separate context, Trump disputed claims that he instructed Vance to initiate peace negotiations with Iran, asserting instead that the vice president’s communication pertained to medical supplies.“Iran needs help with medical supplies. Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well,” Trump informed journalists stationed at Joint Base Andrews when questioned about whether he directed Vance to begin peace talks.This diplomatic push manifests as Trump contemplates a brief, intense new attack directed at Iran following the upcoming US midterm elections.Vance aims to determine whether statecraft can avert another cycle of hostilities, even though the discussions have yet to yield a detailed peace proposal. Rezaei stated during the previous week that Tehran would refuse to negotiate with Washington until its fundamental requirements were satisfied.The diplomatic overture presents a delicate balancing act for Vance, who has publicly backed the war while privately voicing reservations about prolonging it. Prior to Trump launching “Operation Epic Fury” in February, Vance advocated for more robust diplomacy.Trump subsequently designated him lead negotiator, and the vice president undertook international travel on two occasions to confer with Iranian counterparts in pursuit of an agreement to end the conflict.A memorandum of understanding established in June dissolved merely a fortnight after it was signed, caught amid divergent interpretations regarding the restoration of maritime transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Subsequent negotiations facilitated by Qatar and Pakistan have failed to break the deadlock.Washington insists that Tehran provide nuclear concessions upfront, whereas Iranian authorities demand immediate economic relief.Rezaei’s emergence as a key interlocutor threatens to alter the diplomatic framework, potentially sidelining figures such as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. Having served as a veteran of the 1980s war with Iraq and led the IRGC for years, Rezaei has ascended as an influential voice amid mounting threats of renewed US attacks.Earlier this month, he cautioned that Iran could target the United Arab Emirates, alongside regional data centres and internet cables.Trump has alternated between pursuing a diplomatic settlement and threatening to bomb Iran into submission, positioning the dismantling of its nuclear programme as a core national security priority of his second term. He stated last week that Washington was not negotiating with Tehran and suggested military action remained imminent.During a campaign stop on Tuesday, he accused Iran of dragging out efforts to reach a deal and warned that waiting until after the election would not help it.Republican candidates face the prospect of forfeiting seats across the House and Senate during the midterms, with constituents identifying the war and escalating fuel prices among their primary concerns.Consequently, Vance, perceived as an early contender for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, must navigate a conflict carrying both foreign policy and domestic political risks. Trump has maintained that the war will conclude exclusively upon his determination.

news.title: Obama mocks Trump for 'mobilizing whole government' to respond to his Cheesecake Factory joke: 'He was very upset'

Obama mocks Trump for ‘mobilizing whole government' to respond to his Cheesecake Factory joke: 'He was very upset'

Sign up HERE to our DC Insider newsletter for your guide on all the latest from the midterms campaign trail and what's rattling the White House 

By ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER

Published: 01:21 GMT, 29 October 2026 | Updated: 02:03 GMT, 29 October 2026

Former President Barack Obama took the stage in Georgia to campaign for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, with a fresh attack against President Donald Trump.

Obama saved his biggest comedic lines for the White House's reaction to his earlier critiques, escalating a dig where he compared the White House renovations to Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory.

'The President wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,' Obama observed. 'That part didn't bother him - but he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory part.'

Obama claimed he 'mobilized' the whole government over the joke, and continued to describe the response from the administration following the remarks.

'The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy, the person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable, the guy who's supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation and reduce interest rates,' Obama said. 

'They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory!'

Obama also made sharp digs at Trump's cabinet secretaries. Specifically, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

'The defense secretary is laser-focused on very important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops, and live streaming executions because that's how he thinks you cultivate that manly warrior spirit,' Obama remarked.

Opening his critiques, Obama once again poked fun at Trump's extensive remodeling projects at the White House. 

'That guy is building a ballroom that is bigger than the White House. He's paved over the rose garden. Put a helicopter pad on the south lawn, and there is gold everywhere. Take a picture. So much gold,' Obama said to roaring laughter.

'I'm not making this up,' Obama continued. 'He, the President of the United States, is spending time super-gluing gold medallions to the mantle in the Oval Office.'

Obama, often called the Democratic Party's 'closer,' headlined the rally in Atlanta to boost key candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

The former President's visit aims to rally support for Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is seeking reelection against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running against Republican Rick Jackson.

Taking a now infamous jab at the administration's decor, Obama said, 'He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,' a remark delivered despite pushback over the design of his own presidential library in South Side Chicago.

Hitting back on Monday before departing Joint Base Andrews for a campaign event in Mississippi, President Trump insisted his predecessor failed to properly maintain the executive residence, declaring, 'For you to say it's a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.' 

Dismissing Obama's critique, Trump asserted that his predecessor simply does not understand because he is not a 'smart guy.'

'He's not smart at all because of the way he ran the country. Only a stupid person would run the country like that,' Trump said.

'We have to explain that to Obama because he doesn't understand it because he's not a smart guy,' continuing that Obama consistently overlooked 'dirt and filth' and walls that had not 'been cleaned for years.'

During a Saturday campaign appearance for Democrats in Ohio, Obama poked fun at his successor's passion for building projects, remarking that Trump 'should be on HGTV'

'Guys like Obama don't see it... He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building,' Trump argued while defending his updates to the historic residence. 

Firmly standing by his work, the president concluded, 'I've taken care of the White House. I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world,' before adding, 'We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly.'

news.title: Trump, Obama pound campaign trail in closing week of US midterm election
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former President Barack Obama headed to Ohio and Georgia on Wednesday, the sites of critical contests in the Nov 3 midterm election that will determine which party controls the US Congress for the next two years.

The final week of the campaign is playing out at a time when Trump’s public approval rating is near a record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war, threatening Republicans’ majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.

Trump, who has spent the past few weeks on the campaign trail, is set to appear with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces off with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, in one of the most competitive contests that will determine whether Republicans hold their 53-47 advantage in that chamber.

Obama, meanwhile, is due to appear with Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who is facing a challenge by Republican Representative Mike Collins. That state has been so competitive in recent federal election cycles that its three most recent Senate matchups went to runoffs, though this time around nonpartisan analysts view the Democratic incumbent as in a strong position to hold his seat. Obama has kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, when he returned to the campaign trail with blistering speeches criticising his successor.

Americans have been voting for weeks, with more than 36.4 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterms, held in 2022 during Democratic then-President Joe Biden’s term.

Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as likely to be harder fought as Democrats will need to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states, such as Ohio, Iowa or Alaska for the 51 seats they would need for a majority.

“I just think the GOP has lost touch. They dont understand what’s actually going on, and it feels like they’ve broken the promises to people, said Joshua Brazezicke, 26, a property manager from Albrightsville, Pennsylvania, who recently switched his voter registration from independent to Democrat. That state is the site of four highly competitive House races that will play a critical role in determining control of that chamber.

In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energize supporters and boost turnout. Rogers spent the day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating in Imlay City, a small community northeast of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, southwest of Detroit.

news.title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after midterm elections
news.text: WASHINGTON: US officials have told several West Asian countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections in the United States, as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by US diplomats and defense officials.President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.Those threats and the fresh US urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.The White House and US officials declined to comment.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, summarily rejected by Trump, that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to "exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions" and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.The US has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate, leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure..It's unclear how soon the US military would be readyWhile the US has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in West Asia has become more complicated.The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the US.It's unclear how soon after Election Day that the US military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war's end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming "in a couple of weeks, if you don't mind.""Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?" Trump said earlier in the same address. "I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.' It'll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon."Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then -- especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank."Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?" he said..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Mark Carney isn’t the climate hero Europeans think
news.text:
But this rosy view sidesteps a less comfortable reality: Canada is a major fossil fuel producer whose climate ambitions fall far short of Europe’s.

And under Carney, those ambitions are weakening.

Last year, Canada produced more crude oil than any other country outside the big three producers, Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United States. Oil and gas are Canada’s biggest exports by far, and the industry lobby is an influential force in Ottawa.

In his previous life as a central banker, Carney was considered a climate champion. POLITICO even dubbed him an “eco warrior” in 2018. But since taking over as prime minister last year, he has weakened Canada’s climate policies at a rate few predicted, scrapping a national carbon tax and electric vehicle mandate and opening new oil and gas projects.

The list of climate laws Carney has watered down, repealed and canceled makes the EU’s own recent backtracking on green laws look minor. Some environmentalists argue it is comparable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s wholesale dismantling of environmental protections.

“The track the Carney government has taken on climate and environmental regulation has been a decisive move in the direction of the U.S.,” said Tim Gray, executive director of environmental non-profit Environment Defence. Carney, he said, “seems to be all in on fossil fuels.”
news.summary: Canada's prime minister used to be an eco-warrior. Now, not so much.
